Electron g-2 constrains the electron coupling of any 17 MeV boson.

problems.title: An independent third determination of $\alpha$ at 0.1 ppb
problems.plain: With two top measurements disagreeing, a third method that shares none of their possible errors could tell which one is wrong. Candidates use other atoms, such as strontium or ytterbium, or the fine splitting of helium energy levels.
problems.precise: Determine $\alpha$ with relative uncertainty below $10^{-10}$ using a method whose systematics are independent of Raman or Bragg recoil interferometry in alkali atoms, for example single-photon large-momentum-transfer interferometry in Sr or Yb, or helium $2^{3}P$ fine structure, which requires the $\alpha^{8}m$ QED corrections (theory is complete at $\alpha^{7}m$ since 2010) and resolution of the disagreement among helium $2^{3}P$ measurements. The answer is a value of $\alpha^{-1}$ with uncertainty below $1.4 \times 10^{-8}$.
problems.settled_by: Publication of an $\alpha$ value at below $0.1\,\mathrm{ppb}$ from a non-alkali or non-recoil method.

topic_review.cite: L. Morel, Z. Yao, P. Clade, S. Guellati-Khelifa, Determination of the fine-structure constant with an accuracy of 81 parts per trillion, Nature, 2020

problems.title: Certified accuracy of a Hubbard simulator where numerics fail
problems.plain: Once a simulator goes where computers cannot follow, nobody can check its answers by calculation. The task is to bound its errors using only independent calibrations.
problems.precise: Choose a point $(U/t, \delta, T/t)$ where unbiased numerical methods lose control (for example $U/t = 8, \delta = 0.1, T/t < 0.1$). Using Hamiltonian learning of $t, t', U$ and harmonic confinement, entropy thermometry, and stability bounds, give a certified error bar on the nearest-neighbour spin correlator $C(1,0)$ and on the density. Answer: an error budget with all sources listed and a total below $5\%$.
problems.settled_by: A published error budget combining in-situ Hamiltonian calibration with a proof or numerical bound on how parameter errors propagate to local observables.

topic_review.cite: A. Bohrdt, L. Homeier, C. Reinmoser, E. Demler, F. Grusdt, Exploration of doped quantum magnets with ultracold atoms, Annals of Physics, 2021

links.reason: Both require certified error bars for Hubbard observables where unbiased numerics fail.

problems.title: Can cold-atom Hubbard simulators observe d-wave pairing correlations?
problems.plain: In cuprates, electrons form pairs with a four-leaf-clover shape (d-wave) and flow without resistance. The question is whether atoms in an optical lattice, obeying the same model, can be cooled enough to show these pairs.
problems.precise: Two-dimensional square-lattice Fermi-Hubbard model, $U/t = 6\ \text{to}\ 8$, hole doping $\delta = 0.1\ \text{to}\ 0.2$, nearest-neighbour hopping $t$ and optional next-nearest hopping $t'$. Measure the d-wave pair correlation $P_d(r) = \langle \Delta_d^{\mathrm{dag}}(r) \Delta_d(0)\rangle$, with $\Delta_d(r)$ the d-wave singlet pair operator on the four bonds of site r, by quantum gas microscopy or pair-transport protocols at the lowest achievable $T/t$. True long-range order is excluded at $T > 0$ in 2D, so the answer is whether $P_d(r)$ decays algebraically below a Kosterlitz-Thouless temperature $T_{\mathrm{KT}}$, or at least has a correlation length above 10 lattice sites, together with the temperature and entropy at which this appears.
problems.settled_by: A microscope measurement of d-wave pair correlations extending over many sites in a doped, homogeneous Hubbard sample, cross-checked against independent thermometry.
problems.status_note: 2025 experiments reached $T/t = 0.05$ at half filling and resolved a pseudogap in doped samples (arXiv:2502.00095, arXiv:2509.18075), but no d-wave pair correlations have been reported.

topic_review.cite: A. Bohrdt, L. Homeier, C. Reinmoser, E. Demler, F. Grusdt, Exploration of doped quantum magnets with ultracold atoms, Annals of Physics, 2021

links.reason: Simulator d-wave correlations would directly test whether the pure Hubbard model superconducts.

problems.title: Lowest entropy per site reachable in a doped homogeneous Hubbard sample
problems.plain: Pairing in the Hubbard model needs very cold atoms, and the best experiments reached their coldest temperatures only at half filling, one atom per site. The question is how cold a doped sample with holes can be made, and what stops further cooling.
problems.precise: Homogeneous (flat-bottom) 2D square-lattice Fermi-Hubbard sample with at least 100 sites, $U/t = 8$, hole doping $\delta = 0.1\ \text{to}\ 0.2$. Determine the minimum entropy per site $s_{\min}$ (units of $k_{B}$) and temperature $T/t$ reachable by entropy redistribution into reservoirs and adiabatic loading, with independent thermometry, and identify the limiting heating processes (lattice-light scattering, technical noise, reservoir capacity). Answer: $s_{\min}$ and $T/t$ in the doped region with an error budget, and whether $T/t < 0.05$ is reachable at $\delta = 0.125$.
problems.settled_by: A doped homogeneous sample with thermometry validated against finite-temperature numerics, plus a measured heating budget.
problems.status_note: A 2025 experiment reached $T/t = 0.05 (+0.06/-0.05)$ at half filling by entropy redistribution (Xu et al., Nature 642, 909, arXiv:2502.00095).

topic_review.cite: A. Bohrdt, L. Homeier, C. Reinmoser, E. Demler, F. Grusdt, Exploration of doped quantum magnets with ultracold atoms, Annals of Physics, 2021

problems.title: Entropy reduction needed to see d-wave correlations in Hubbard simulators
problems.plain: Cooling atoms in a lattice is limited by how much disorder (entropy) remains per site. The question is how far below today's best entropy an experiment must go before pairing becomes visible.
problems.precise: Let $s_{\exp}$ be the entropy per site (units of $k_B$) reached in current doped quantum-gas-microscope samples. For the 2D Hubbard model at $U/t = 8$, $\delta = 0.125$, $t'/t = -0.2$, determine the entropy per site $s*$ below which the d-wave pair correlation length exceeds 10 lattice sites, and hence the required reduction $s_{\exp} - s*$. Answer: $s*$ with error bars from controlled finite-temperature numerics and the ratio $s_{\exp}/s*$.
problems.settled_by: Controlled finite-temperature numerics (for example diagrammatic Monte Carlo or tensor-network methods with error bars) giving the pair correlation length as a function of entropy per site at the stated parameters.
problems.status_note: Ground-state DMRG and auxiliary-field quantum Monte Carlo find d-wave order coexisting with partially filled stripes at $t' \ne 0$ (Xu et al., Science 2024); controlled finite-temperature values of $s*$ are lacking.

topic_review.cite: A. Bohrdt, L. Homeier, C. Reinmoser, E. Demler, F. Grusdt, Exploration of doped quantum magnets with ultracold atoms, Annals of Physics, 2021

problems.title: Does cold-atom Hubbard resistivity stay linear in temperature at low T?
problems.plain: Many cuprates show electrical resistance growing in proportion to temperature, unlike ordinary metals. Atom experiments saw this down to moderate temperatures, and it is unknown whether it continues when the atoms are colder.
problems.precise: In the doped 2D Hubbard model at $U/t = 8$, $\delta = 0.1 \text{ to } 0.2$, measure the resistivity $\rho(T)$ from charge-current relaxation or from density diffusion via the Nernst-Einstein relation for $T/t$ from 1 down to 0.1. Answer: whether $\rho \sim T$ persists below $T = 0.3 t$ and whether the transport rate approaches the Planckian value $\hbar/\tau \sim k_B T$.
problems.settled_by: Transport measurements at T/t below 0.3 with independent thermometry, compared with finite-temperature numerics.
problems.status_note: Brown et al. (Science 2019) found $T$-linear resistivity above the Mott-Ioffe-Regel limit (the resistivity at which the mean free path equals one lattice spacing) at $U/t = 7.4$, $n = 0.82$, for $T/t$ from about 0.3 to 8; no data exist below about $0.3\,t$.

topic_review.cite: A. Bohrdt, L. Homeier, C. Reinmoser, E. Demler, F. Grusdt, Exploration of doped quantum magnets with ultracold atoms, Annals of Physics, 2021

links.reason: Cold-atom Hubbard resistivity isolates whether T-linear transport arises without phonons or disorder.

problems.title: Do spin-charge stripes appear in an isotropic two-dimensional Hubbard simulator?
problems.plain: In some cuprates the holes line up in rows separated by magnetic stripes. Atom experiments saw stripes form in a simplified version of the model where holes move only along one direction; the full two-dimensional case has not shown them.
problems.precise: Square-lattice Fermi-Hubbard model with isotropic hopping, $U/t = 8 \text{ to } 10$, $\delta = 1/8$, $t'/t = 0 \text{ and } -0.2$, imaged by quantum gas microscopy. Measure spin-spin and hole-hole correlation functions and determine whether unidirectional stripe correlations with wavelength set by the doping appear at the lowest accessible $T/t$ (about 0.05 to 0.1). Answer: stripe correlation length versus $T/t$ and $t'$, compared with finite-temperature numerics.
problems.settled_by: Microscope snapshots of a doped isotropic 2D lattice showing stripe correlations over several periods, matched to numerics at the measured temperature.
problems.status_note: Individual stripes were observed in a mixed-dimensional Fermi-Hubbard system in which holes hop only along one axis (Bourgund et al., Nature 2025, doi:10.1038/s41586-024-08270-7); no isotropic 2D observation was found in a 2026 arXiv search.

topic_review.cite: A. Bohrdt, L. Homeier, C. Reinmoser, E. Demler, F. Grusdt, Exploration of doped quantum magnets with ultracold atoms, Annals of Physics, 2021

links.reason: Stripes in an isotropic Hubbard simulator test whether cuprate charge order is intrinsic.

problems.title: Does antihydrogen 1S-2S match hydrogen at $10^{-15}$?
problems.plain: Antihydrogen (an antiproton bound to a positron) should have exactly the same energy levels as hydrogen if matter and antimatter mirror each other perfectly. The main ultraviolet line has been compared to a few parts in $10^{12}$; hydrogen itself is known about a thousand times better.
problems.precise: ALPHA measured the antihydrogen $1\mathrm{S}-2\mathrm{S}$ two-photon frequency in agreement with hydrogen at about $2 \times 10^{-12}$ relative precision (2018). Determine whether nu_1S2S(Hbar) - nu_1S2S(H) is nonzero at the $10^{-15}$ level, approaching the hydrogen precision of about 4e-15.
problems.settled_by: Antihydrogen 1S-2S spectroscopy with laser-cooled, magnetically trapped atoms reaching sub-kHz resolution and $10^{-15}$ accuracy.
problems.status_note: ALPHA demonstrated laser cooling of antihydrogen in 2021, a prerequisite for the next precision step.

topic_review.cite: V. A. Kostelecky, N. Russell, Data tables for Lorentz and CPT violation, Reviews of Modern Physics, 2011

problems.title: Antihydrogen ground-state hyperfine splitting at the ppm level
problems.plain: The tiny splitting caused by the magnetic interaction of the antiproton and positron is sensitive to different possible symmetry violations than the optical line. It has been measured only to a few parts in 10000.
problems.precise: Measure the zero-field ground-state hyperfine splitting of antihydrogen (hydrogen: 1420.405751768 MHz) with relative uncertainty below $10^{-6}$, using either an in-beam Rabi method (ASACUSA) or trapped-atom microwave spectroscopy (ALPHA), and determine whether it differs from hydrogen.
problems.settled_by: A beam or trap measurement of the Hbar hyperfine splitting with ppm uncertainty compared to the hydrogen maser value.

topic_review.cite: V. A. Kostelecky, N. Russell, Data tables for Lorentz and CPT violation, Reviews of Modern Physics, 2011

problems.title: Proton and antiproton magnetic moments compared at $10^{-12}$
problems.plain: A single proton or antiproton held in an electromagnetic trap can have its magnetism measured by flipping its spin. Matter-antimatter symmetry requires the two magnetic moments to be equal and opposite.
problems.precise: BASE compared proton and antiproton charge-to-mass ratios to 16 ppt (2022) and magnetic moments to about 1.5 ppb (2017). Determine whether $\left|\mu_{\mathrm{pbar}}\right|/\mu_{\mathrm{p}} - 1$ is nonzero at the $10^{-12}$ level, using sympathetic or quantum-logic cooling for faster single-spin-flip detection.
problems.settled_by: Penning-trap measurements of the proton and antiproton g-factors each at sub-ppt uncertainty.

topic_review.cite: V. A. Kostelecky, N. Russell, Data tables for Lorentz and CPT violation, Reviews of Modern Physics, 2011

problems.title: Are electron-sector Lorentz-violation coefficients nonzero at $10^{-23}$?
problems.plain: If space had a preferred direction, an electron moving in an atom would have slightly different energy depending on how the atom is oriented as the Earth rotates. Clocks with oddly shaped electron orbitals are the most sensitive detectors of this.
problems.precise: In the Standard-Model Extension, the electron coefficients $c_{JK}$ (traceless symmetric) are bounded at about $10^{-21}$ by Yb+ E3 clock comparisons with orthogonal quantization axes (Sanner et al 2019). Determine whether any $c_{JK}$ is nonzero at the $10^{-23}$ level using highly charged ions or Dy and Yb+ states with large anisotropic momentum operators.
problems.settled_by: Sidereal-modulation analysis of a clock comparison with anisotropy sensitivity enhanced by more than 100 over Yb+ E3.

topic_review.cite: V. A. Kostelecky, N. Russell, Data tables for Lorentz and CPT violation, Reviews of Modern Physics, 2011

links.reason: Laboratory and astrophysical bounds constrain the same Lorentz-violating effective-field-theory coefficients.

problems.title: Can massive superpositions exclude the GRW collapse rate?
problems.plain: Collapse models modify quantum mechanics so that large objects lose superpositions on their own. The original proposed rate has never been ruled out.
problems.precise: Continuous spontaneous localization with rate $\lambda$ and length $r_C$. Exclude $\lambda = 10^{-16}\ \mathrm{s}^{-1}$ at $r_C = 10^{-5}\ \mathrm{cm}$ (the GRW value of Ghirardi, Rimini and Weber) by interferometric or non-interferometric (heating, noise) tests with massive objects. Answer: yes or no, with the excluded region in the $(\lambda, r_C)$ plane.
problems.settled_by: An interferometry or heating experiment whose excess-decoherence bound lies below $\lambda$ = $10^{-16}$ $\mathrm{s}^{-1}$ at $r_C$ = $10^{-5}$ cm.
problems.status_note: Non-interferometric tests (to 2021) constrain the enhanced Adler rates, and 2025 interference of sodium clusters above 170,000 amu (Pedalino et al., arXiv:2507.21211) tightened interferometric bounds; the GRW point is not reported excluded, which should be checked against the 2025 exclusion plot.

parents.note: Excluding the GRW point is one point of closing the CSL window

problems.title: What limits mechanical cat-state coherence as mass grows?
problems.plain: A 16-microgram vibrating crystal has been put into a cat state, a superposition of two distinct motions. The question is whether its decay is fully explained by known noise, or whether something extra appears at larger mass.
problems.precise: Mechanical resonator of effective mass $m_{\mathrm{eff}}$ in a cat state $\left|\alpha\right> + \left|-\alpha\right>$. Measure the cat decoherence rate $\Gamma_{\mathrm{cat}}$ versus $\mid\alpha\mid^2$ and $m_{\mathrm{eff}}$, and compare with the bath model $\Gamma_{\mathrm{cat}} = 2 \mid\alpha\mid^2 \Gamma_{\mathrm{m}} (2 n_{\mathrm{th}} + 1)$, with $\Gamma_{\mathrm{m}}$ the mechanical energy damping rate and $n_{\mathrm{th}}$ the thermal phonon number, plus two-level-system defect noise. Answer: whether all decoherence is accounted for, and any excess as a function of mass.
problems.settled_by: Systematic Wigner-function tomography of cats across masses and separations with independently measured bath parameters.
problems.status_note: Cat states of a 16-microgram oscillator were reported in 2023 (Bild et al., Science).

topic_review.cite: M. Aspelmeyer, T. J. Kippenberg, F. Marquardt, Cavity optomechanics, Reviews of Modern Physics, 2014

links.reason: Mass-dependent cat decoherence is the observable separating Diosi-Penrose collapse from environmental noise.
Classical-gravity models predict mass-dependent decoherence bounded by massive cat coherence times.
Leggett-Garg tests on massive oscillators need cat coherence that survives growing mass.

problems.title: First measurement of the parity-violating energy difference between enantiomers
problems.plain: The left- and right-handed forms of a chiral molecule should differ in energy by a tiny amount because of the weak force. No experiment has yet been sensitive enough to see it.
problems.precise:
$\Delta E_{\mathrm{PV}} = E(R) - E(S)$ between enantiomers, or the corresponding difference in a vibrational or rotational transition frequency, $\Delta 
u/
u$. The best direct bound is at the $10^{-13}$ level of relative frequency for the C-F stretch of CHFClBr (Daussy et al., PRL 1999), several orders of magnitude above predictions for that molecule; heavy-atom candidates (Re, Os, Ru, W complexes, scaling roughly as $Z^5$) are predicted to be larger. An answer is a nonzero $\Delta 
u$ or $\Delta E_{\mathrm{PV}}$ with significance above $5\,\sigma$, with sign and magnitude compared to theory.
problems.settled_by: Ultrastable-laser vibrational spectroscopy of both enantiomers of a heavy-atom chiral molecule, or a time-resolved measurement of parity evolution in parity-selected states, reaching the predicted $\Delta E_{\mathrm{PV}}$.
problems.status_note: Experiments with cold molecular beams and heavy-atom candidates were still described as progress toward detection in 2025 (Phys. Chem. Chem. Phys. 2025).

topic_review.cite: M. Quack, J. Stohner and M. Willeke, High-resolution spectroscopic studies and theory of parity violation in chiral molecules, Annual Review of Physical Chemistry, 2008

problems.title: Can parity violation bias the homochirality of biological molecules?
problems.plain: Life uses only left-handed amino acids and right-handed sugars, and the weak force slightly favors one handedness. The favoring is predicted to be extremely small, and it is unknown whether any natural chemical process could amplify it into a full preference.
problems.precise: Predicted $\Delta E_{\mathrm{PV}}$ for amino acids and sugars corresponds to an equilibrium enantiomeric excess of order $10^{-17}$ at $300\,\mathrm{K}$ (estimate). Question: does any autocatalytic amplification mechanism (Frank-type autocatalysis with mutual inhibition, Kondepudi-Nelson bifurcation, Viedma ripening) under prebiotic conditions convert a bias of this size into a probability of selecting the natural handedness measurably different from $1/2$, given statistical fluctuations of order $N^{-1/2}$ in $N$ molecules and competing chiral biases (circularly polarized light, magnetochiral effects). An answer is a model with measured rate constants and volumes giving that probability, or an experiment showing PV-directed selection.
problems.settled_by: A calculation of the selection probability in a chemically realistic amplification network with measured parameters, together with an accurate $\Delta E_{\mathrm{PV}}$ for the relevant molecules.
problems.status_note: Theoretical estimates place the PV-induced excess near $10^{-17}$ at 300 K; no experiment has shown PV-directed selection.

topic_review.cite: M. Quack, J. Stohner and M. Willeke, High-resolution spectroscopic studies and theory of parity violation in chiral molecules, Annual Review of Physical Chemistry, 2008

parents.note: Parity violation is one candidate symmetry-breaking bias for biological homochirality

problems.title: What stabilizes enantiomers: parity violation or environmental decoherence?
problems.plain: Quantum mechanics without the weak force says a chiral molecule's true lowest state is an equal mix of left and right forms, yet real chiral molecules stay left or right for practical eternity. Whether the weak force or the molecule's surroundings fixes the handedness is still debated for molecules where the two effects are comparable.
problems.precise: For a chiral molecule with tunneling splitting $\Delta_{+-}$ between parity eigenstates, chirality is stable if $\Delta E_{\mathrm{PV}} >> \Delta_{+-}$ (weak force dominates) or if environmental decoherence and collisions localize the state. Question: for molecules where $\Delta_{+-}$ and $\Delta E_{\mathrm{PV}}$ are comparable (proposed: ClSSCl and related axially chiral molecules), which mechanism controls the observed time evolution, and at what $\Delta_{+-} / \Delta E_{\mathrm{PV}}$ and collision rate does the crossover occur. An answer is a measured time evolution of parity or chirality in such a molecule under controlled collision rates, matched by theory.
problems.settled_by: Gas-phase or molecular-beam measurement of parity-state evolution in a molecule with $\Delta_{+-}$ near $\Delta E_{\mathrm{PV}}$, at variable pressure.
problems.status_note: For molecules with large barriers decoherence and $\Delta E_{\mathrm{PV}}$ both explain stability; the comparable regime remains untested experimentally.

topic_review.cite: M. Quack, J. Stohner and M. Willeke, High-resolution spectroscopic studies and theory of parity violation in chiral molecules, Annual Review of Physical Chemistry, 2008

links.reason: Chiral-state stability is a test case of environment-induced selection of classical states.

problems.title: Nuclear anapole moments from molecular spectroscopy
problems.plain: The weak force inside a nucleus produces a tiny magnetic feature called the anapole moment, measured so far only for cesium atoms. Polar molecules amplify this effect and could measure it for other nuclei, testing how the weak force acts between protons and neutrons.
problems.precise: Nuclear-spin-dependent parity violation in diatomic molecules (BaF with Ba-137, TlF, RaF and others) measured by tuning opposite-parity rotational-hyperfine levels near degeneracy with a magnetic field; the observable is the matrix element $W_A k_A$, with $W_A$ computed by electronic structure and $k_A$ dominated by the anapole moment. The only measured anapole (Cs-133, Wood et al. 1997) yields weak meson-nucleon couplings that disagree with other hadronic parity-violation data. An answer is $k_A$ for at least one more nucleus with uncertainty below about 20 percent and a test of the Cs inconsistency.
problems.settled_by: A molecular-beam or laser-cooled-molecule measurement of the parity-violating mixing of near-degenerate levels giving a nonzero $W_{A} k_{A}$ for a nucleus other than Cs-133.
problems.status_note: Sensitivity of the method was demonstrated in 2018 (Altuntas et al., PRL); laser-cooled BaF (Kogel et al., Phys. Rev. Research 2025) and TlF schemes (2023) are in development.

topic_review.cite: M. Quack, J. Stohner and M. Willeke, High-resolution spectroscopic studies and theory of parity violation in chiral molecules, Annual Review of Physical Chemistry, 2008

problems.title: Accuracy of relativistic predictions of molecular parity-violating energies
problems.plain: Calculations of the left-right energy difference must include relativity, electron correlation and molecular vibrations, and different methods can give answers differing by large factors. A trusted value with an error bar is needed before an experiment can test the weak force.
problems.precise: $\Delta E_{\mathrm{PV}}$ from the nuclear-spin-independent electron-nucleus weak interaction H_PV = (G_F / (2 sqrt 2)) sum_A Q_W(A) sum_i gamma_5(i) rho_A(r_i), computed with four-component Dirac-Coulomb or two-component Hamiltonians at DFT and coupled-cluster levels, including vibrational averaging and large-amplitude torsional motion. Question: for a chosen experimental candidate (e.g. CHFClBr, a Re or Os complex), what is $\Delta E_{\mathrm{PV}}$ and the vibrational-frequency difference with a total uncertainty below about 20 percent. An answer is converged values with error bars from at least two independent correlated relativistic methods.
problems.settled_by: Systematic four-component coupled-cluster calculations with vibrational averaging that agree with an independent method within the stated error for a molecule under experimental study.
problems.status_note: A 2025 study (Sunaga et al., J. Chem. Phys.) found strong parity-violation effects from large-amplitude motions, showing that vibrational treatment can change predictions substantially.

topic_review.cite: M. Quack, J. Stohner and M. Willeke, High-resolution spectroscopic studies and theory of parity violation in chiral molecules, Annual Review of Physical Chemistry, 2008

problems.title: Fine-structure anomaly of 2p levels in heavy muonic atoms
problems.plain: In muonic atoms of heavy elements such as zirconium, tin and lead, the measured gap between two closely spaced muon levels disagreed with theory for decades. Distortion of the nucleus by the muon turned out too small to explain it, and a 2025 calculation blames an incomplete treatment of the recoil of the nucleus instead.
problems.precise: The measured 2p_3/2 - 2p_1/2 fine-structure splittings in muonic Zr-90, Sn-120 and Pb-208 could not be fitted together with the other muonic X-ray lines using one nuclear charge distribution per nucleus; nuclear polarization does not account for the deviation (Valuev et al, arXiv 2201.09638). A treatment including relativistic nuclear recoil (Beyer et al, arXiv 2511.22298) reports consistent fits for Zr-90 and Sn-120, with r_rms(Zr-90) = 4.2732(7) fm, about $3\sigma$ above the accepted value. Determine whether the same treatment removes the anomaly in Pb-208 and whether the shifted charge radii are confirmed by independent data.
problems.settled_by: A single theory framework that reproduces all measured muonic X-ray energies of Zr-90, Sn-120 and Pb-208 within experimental uncertainty with one nuclear charge distribution per nucleus, checked against new high-resolution muonic X-ray data or electron scattering radii.
problems.status_note: A November 2025 preprint (arXiv 2511.22298) reports that relativistic recoil resolves the Zr-90 anomaly and gives a consistent result for Sn-120; Pb-208 and independent confirmation remain open.

topic_review.cite: R. Pohl, R. Gilman, G. A. Miller, K. Pachucki, Muonic hydrogen and the proton radius puzzle, Annual Review of Nuclear and Particle Science, 2013

problems.title: Ground-state hyperfine splitting of muonic hydrogen at the ppm level
problems.plain: In muonic hydrogen the muon orbits very close to the proton, so the small magnetic splitting of its lowest level depends on how charge and magnetism are spread inside the proton. This splitting has never been measured directly, and several experiments are now trying.
problems.precise: Measure the $1\mathrm{S}$ hyperfine transition of muonic hydrogen (about 0.18 eV, mid-infrared wavelength near 6.8 micron) with relative uncertainty of order $10^{-5}$ (FAMU goal) to $10^{-6}$ (CREMA goal), and extract the proton Zemach radius $r_Z$ and the polarizability part of the two-photon-exchange correction. The answer is $r_Z$ with uncertainty below 1% and a statement of whether it agrees with values from electron scattering and from the hydrogen 21 cm hyperfine splitting.
problems.settled_by: A laser-spectroscopy measurement of the muonic hydrogen 1S hyperfine transition at ppm or 10 ppm uncertainty, combined with a two-photon-exchange calculation of matching precision.
problems.status_note: FAMU reported first operation at the RIKEN-RAL muon facility at ISIS in 2025 (arXiv 2509.10350) and CREMA is preparing a pulsed-laser measurement at PSI (arXiv 2211.08297); no measured value has been published as of mid-2026.

topic_review.cite: R. Pohl, R. Gilman, G. A. Miller, K. Pachucki, Muonic hydrogen and the proton radius puzzle, Annual Review of Nuclear and Particle Science, 2013

links.reason: Muonic hyperfine splitting requires the proton Zemach radius and polarizability contributions.

problems.title: Muonium hyperfine and 1S-2S intervals at improved precision
problems.plain: Muonium, an antimuon holding an electron, contains no proton, so its energy levels test the theory of light and charges without nuclear-structure uncertainty and give the muon mass and magnetism. Its best measurements date from about 25 years ago.
problems.precise: The muonium ground-state hyperfine interval (about $4.463\,\mathrm{GHz}$) was last measured at LAMPF in 1999 and the $1\mathrm{S}-2\mathrm{S}$ two-photon interval at RAL in 2000. Improve both by at least a factor of 10 (MuSEUM at J-PARC for the hyperfine interval, Mu-MASS at PSI for $1\mathrm{S}-2\mathrm{S}$) and determine $m_\mu/m_e$ and $\mu_\mu/\mu_p$ from them, testing whether the two routes and QED theory agree.
problems.settled_by: New muonium hyperfine and $1\mathrm{S}-2\mathrm{S}$ measurements, each with an uncertainty at least ten times below the 1999-2000 values, combined with bound-state QED theory to yield consistent $m_{\mu}/m_e$ values.
problems.status_note: MuSEUM reported ongoing hyperfine measurements at J-PARC aiming at a tenfold improvement in 2025 (arXiv 2501.02736).

topic_review.cite: R. Pohl, R. Gilman, G. A. Miller, K. Pachucki, Muonic hydrogen and the proton radius puzzle, Annual Review of Nuclear and Particle Science, 2013

links.reason: Muonium hyperfine data fix the muon magnetic moment ratio used to extract g-2.

problems.title: Atom interferometry determination of G at 10 ppm
problems.plain: Atoms in free fall make test masses that cannot twist, stretch or be magnetized like a pendulum fiber, so they could give G free of the usual suspects. Their best result so far is about ten times less precise than needed.
problems.precise: Atom-interferometric gravity gradiometry with well-characterized source masses gave G with about 150 ppm uncertainty (Rosi et al 2014). Determine G with uncertainty below $10^{-5}$ relative by a cold-atom method, sufficient to discriminate among the discrepant macroscopic results.
problems.settled_by: A cold-atom G measurement with total uncertainty below 10 ppm and a published complete error budget.

topic_review.cite: C. Rothleitner, S. Schlamminger, Invited Review Article: Measurements of the Newtonian constant of gravitation, G, Review of Scientific Instruments, 2017

problems.title: Why laboratory values of G scatter beyond their stated uncertainties
problems.plain: About a dozen top experiments, each claiming an error of a few parts in 100000, give values of G that spread by about 5 parts in 10000. Something in how G is measured is not understood.
problems.precise: Laboratory determinations of G (torsion balances in time-of-swing, angular-acceleration and servo modes, beam balances, simple pendulums, atom interferometry) spread over about $5 \times 10^{-4}$ relative, roughly ten times their typical quoted uncertainties of $10^{-5} \text{ to } 5 \times 10^{-5}$, near $G = 6.674 \times 10^{-8}\,\mathrm{cm}^{3}\,\mathrm{g}^{-1}\,\mathrm{s}^{-2}$. Identify the unaccounted systematic effects (or establish any genuine dependence of the measured G on method, material or geometry) that explain the excess scatter.
problems.settled_by: A consensus set of independent measurements with different methods agreeing within quoted uncertainties at the $10^{-5}$ level, together with an identified correction to the outliers.
problems.status_note: NIST published a 10-year blinded torsion-balance result in Metrologia in 2026 that lies about 235 ppm below the BIPM value obtained with the same apparatus design.

topic_review.cite: C. Rothleitner, S. Schlamminger, Invited Review Article: Measurements of the Newtonian constant of gravitation, G, Review of Scientific Instruments, 2017

problems.title: Same apparatus design, different G: the NIST versus BIPM discrepancy
problems.plain: NIST rebuilt the instrument used by the international measurement bureau (BIPM) and got a value about 2 parts in 10000 lower. Since the design is the same, the difference should be traceable to a specific cause.
problems.precise: The NIST measurement (2026, Metrologia), using a torsion-strip balance of the BIPM design in both servo and Cavendish modes, gives $G = 6.67387 \times 10^{-8}\,\mathrm{cm}^3\,\mathrm{g}^{-1}\,\mathrm{s}^{-2}$, about 235 ppm below the BIPM 2013 value. Identify the effect (mass metrology, torsion-strip anelasticity, source-mass density inhomogeneity, alignment, environment) that accounts for the difference.
problems.settled_by: A cross-check with exchanged source masses or fibers, or a third realization of the same apparatus, that isolates the component responsible for the 235 ppm offset.
problems.status_note: NIST's blinded result was unblinded in July 2024 and published in April 2026.

topic_review.cite: C. Rothleitner, S. Schlamminger, Invited Review Article: Measurements of the Newtonian constant of gravitation, G, Review of Scientific Instruments, 2017

problems.title: Optimal scaling of atomic-clock stability with atom number under laser noise
problems.plain: A clock steers a laser using N atoms, but the laser itself jitters, which limits how long atoms can be probed. The best possible improvement from entangling the atoms, given this jitter, is not known.
problems.precise: For a Ramsey-type optical clock with $N$ atoms and local-oscillator frequency noise with power spectrum $S(f)\sim h_\alpha f^{-\alpha} (\alpha=0, 1, 2)$, determine the optimal asymptotic scaling with $N$ of the long-term Allan deviation $\sigma_y(\tau)$, optimizing over entangled states, adaptive measurements and feedback, and whether any protocol reaches $1/N$ scaling up to logarithmic factors.
problems.settled_by: A matching lower bound and explicit protocol for the Allan deviation exponent as a function of N for each noise type.
problems.status_note: Protocols with near-Heisenberg scaling up to logarithmic factors are known for white phase noise; matching bounds for 1/f and random-walk laser noise are lacking.

topic_review.cite: R. Demkowicz-Dobrzanski, J. Kolodynski, M. Guta, The elusive Heisenberg limit in quantum-enhanced metrology, Nature Communications, 2012

problems.title: Precision scaling under spatially correlated and non-Markovian dephasing
problems.plain: Real noise often hits all atoms together or has memory in time. How the best achievable precision then scales with particle number and time is known only in special cases.
problems.precise: For $N$ qubits sensing a phase under dephasing with spatial correlation function $C(r)$ and temporal spectrum $S(\omega)$, including the non-Markovian Zeno regime, classify the asymptotic scaling exponent of the minimal estimation error with $N$ and total time $T$, and identify the states and measurements attaining it.
problems.settled_by: Bounds and attaining protocols covering the main classes of correlated noise, with matching exponents.

topic_review.cite: R. Demkowicz-Dobrzanski, J. Kolodynski, M. Guta, The elusive Heisenberg limit in quantum-enhanced metrology, Nature Communications, 2012

links.reason: Spatially correlated noise threatens both Heisenberg scaling and the fault-tolerance threshold.

problems.title: Can entanglement improve a clock already at the stability frontier?
problems.plain: Squeezed atom states (correlated states with reduced noise in one quantity) have beaten the standard limit in clocks, but only in setups that were not the most stable clocks available. The question is whether entanglement can improve the very best clocks in absolute terms.
problems.precise: Demonstrate an optical lattice or tweezer clock whose absolute fractional frequency instability, with entangled or squeezed atomic states, is below that of the best unentangled clock with the same atom number and interrogation hardware, at instability levels of order $10^{-17}$ at 1 s or better.
problems.settled_by: A clock comparison showing an entanglement-enabled absolute stability improvement over the unentangled state of the art.
problems.status_note: Spin squeezing in optical clocks gave gains of a few dB below the standard quantum limit in differential comparisons (2023-2024), not an absolute record.

topic_review.cite: R. Demkowicz-Dobrzanski, J. Kolodynski, M. Guta, The elusive Heisenberg limit in quantum-enhanced metrology, Nature Communications, 2012

problems.title: Heisenberg scaling with error correction under imperfect control
problems.plain: Quantum error correction can restore the ideal 1/N gain when the signal and the noise act differently on the sensor. It is open in general whether this still works when the correcting operations are themselves noisy.
problems.precise: For a sensor Hamiltonian $H$ and Markovian noise with Lindblad operators $L_k$ obeying the HNLS condition ($H \text{ not in } \operatorname{span}\{1, L_k, L_k^{\mathrm{dag}}, L_k^{\mathrm{dag}} L_j\}, 1 = \text{identity}$), a fault-tolerant threshold for Heisenberg scaling is known for a Pauli-Z signal under bit-flip noise with a repetition code and noisy state preparation and measurement (Sahu, Xu, Zhou, arXiv 2601.05457, 2026). Determine whether a threshold exists for every HNLS-satisfying noise model with noisy ancillas, syndrome extraction and recovery, and how the qubit and time overhead scales with $N$ and the target precision.
problems.settled_by: A proof of a threshold theorem for metrology with fault-tolerant recovery covering general HNLS noise, or a counterexample noise model for which precision saturates at any nonzero control-error rate.
problems.status_note: A January 2026 preprint (arXiv 2601.05457) proves Heisenberg scaling below a threshold for repetition-code protocols with noisy operations; general noise models, overheads and experiments beyond a few qubits remain open.

topic_review.cite: R. Demkowicz-Dobrzanski, J. Kolodynski, M. Guta, The elusive Heisenberg limit in quantum-enhanced metrology, Nature Communications, 2012

problems.title: Can local dissipation prepare a pure chiral topological state?
problems.plain: Engineered loss can pump atoms into a chosen state, like water settling at the bottom of a bowl. It is unknown whether this works for states with a built-in handedness, such as the quantum Hall states, using only short-range processes.
problems.precise: Fermions or spins on a 2D lattice evolving under a Lindblad master equation with finite-range jump operators and finite-range Hamiltonian. Determine whether a pure state with nonzero Chern number (or nonzero Hall conductance) can be the unique steady state with a Liouvillian gap that stays finite as $N \to \infty$. Known obstructions: quadratic (Gaussian) local Lindbladians cannot do it (Budich, Zoller, Diehl, PRA 2015), and local commuting-projector Hamiltonians have zero Hall conductance (Kapustin, Fidkowski, CMP 2019). Answer: a general no-go proof covering interacting Lindbladians, or an explicit local Lindbladian that works.
problems.settled_by: A theorem extending the Gaussian obstruction to interacting finite-range Lindbladians, or a constructed counterexample with a proven size-independent Liouvillian gap.
problems.status_note: Approximate dissipative schemes for Chern and fractional Chern insulators exist (Liu, Bergholtz, Budich, Phys. Rev. Research 2021), but none gives an exact pure chiral steady state with a finite gap.

topic_review.cite: L. M. Sieberer, M. Buchhold, J. Marino, S. Diehl, Universality in driven open quantum matter, Reviews of Modern Physics, 2025

problems.title: Universality classes of dissipative phase transitions in atomic gases
problems.plain: Driven atoms that also lose energy can switch abruptly between collective states. Whether these switches follow the same laws as ordinary phase transitions is unknown.
problems.precise: Continuous transitions in Markovian driven-dissipative atomic systems (driven Rydberg gases, pumped condensates) in $d = 2\ \text{or}\ 3$. Determine critical exponents and whether they coincide with equilibrium classes at an effective temperature or form new classes, such as the independent coherence exponent predicted by Sieberer et al., PRL 2013. Answer: measured exponents and class.
problems.settled_by: Measured critical exponents near a continuous dissipative transition, including a dynamical exponent absent in equilibrium.

topic_review.cite: L. M. Sieberer, M. Buchhold, J. Marino, S. Diehl, Universality in driven open quantum matter, Reviews of Modern Physics, 2025

parents.note: Atomic-gas dissipative transitions are instances of the general non-equilibrium class question

problems.title: Do exceptional points improve sensing once quantum noise is counted?
problems.plain: At special points (exceptional points, where two modes of a lossy system merge) a sensor's response grows faster than normal with the signal, but its noise grows too. Whether there is a net gain is debated.
problems.precise: Sensor operated near an order-n exceptional point, where frequency splitting scales as $\epsilon^{1/n}$. Including quantum noise, Petermann excess noise and gain or loss, compare the quantum Fisher information per unit time and per photon with that of the best Hermitian sensor of equal loss. Answer: yes or no for a fundamental advantage, with conditions.
problems.settled_by: A general bound on Fisher information near exceptional points, tested by an atomic or optical experiment at the quantum noise limit.
problems.status_note: Theoretical analyses since 2018 (Lau and Clerk; Langbein) find no generic advantage for some schemes and possible gains for nonreciprocal ones.

topic_review.cite: L. M. Sieberer, M. Buchhold, J. Marino, S. Diehl, Universality in driven open quantum matter, Reviews of Modern Physics, 2025

problems.title: Universality class of the Rydberg facilitation absorbing-state transition
problems.plain: In a gas where one excited Rydberg atom makes it easier for its neighbours to get excited, excitations spread like an epidemic or die out. The question is whether this switch follows the same laws as the standard model of spreading, called directed percolation.
problems.precise: Atoms driven off resonance at detuning $\Delta$ chosen to meet the facilitation (anti-blockade) condition, with Rydberg decay rate $\gamma$ and spontaneous seeding rate, in $d = 2\ \mathrm{or}\ 3$. In the frozen-gas limit the active-to-absorbing transition is predicted to be in the directed-percolation class, while atomic motion gives anomalous directed percolation or mean-field behaviour (Brady et al., arXiv:2404.16523). Measure the critical exponents $\beta$ (order parameter) and $\delta$ (density decay at criticality) and test whether the self-tuning to the critical point reported by Helmrich et al. (Nature 2020) is self-organized criticality in the strict sense. Answer: exponents with error bars and the class they identify.
problems.settled_by: Measured critical exponents of excitation density versus time and drive in the frozen-gas limit, matched to directed-percolation values within error bars.
problems.status_note: A 2025 theory and experiment study on cold Rb used avalanche distributions to identify a crossover from directed percolation to mean-field behaviour on a dynamic network of moving atoms (Ohler et al., arXiv:2502.14757); clean exponents in the frozen limit are not established.

topic_review.cite: L. M. Sieberer, M. Buchhold, J. Marino, S. Diehl, Universality in driven open quantum matter, Reviews of Modern Physics, 2025

links.reason: Adding coherence to facilitation gives the quantum contact process; both ask about DP.
Rydberg facilitation offers a clean directed-percolation test where most experiments fail.

problems.title: Do two-body losses create long-range magnetic correlations in Hubbard lattices?
problems.plain: Removing pairs of atoms that occupy the same lattice site leaves the survivors in special spin arrangements. Small double-well experiments saw the magnetic correlations flip sign, and whether this grows into extended magnetic order in a full lattice is open.
problems.precise: Two-component fermions in a 2D optical lattice described by the Hubbard model $(t, U)$ plus engineered on-site two-body loss at rate $\gamma$ (for example by photoassociation). Starting from an antiferromagnetically correlated state, determine the time evolution of the spin correlation function $C(r)$ of the surviving atoms, whether nearest-neighbour correlations reverse sign as predicted for double wells, and whether the reversed correlations extend beyond one lattice spacing, as functions of $\gamma/t$ and $U/t$. Answer: $C(r, \mathrm{time})$ measured and reproduced by Lindblad numerics.
problems.settled_by: Quantum gas microscope measurements of C(r) in a lossy 2D lattice compared with full Lindblad simulation.
problems.status_note: Sign reversal of the magnetic correlation was observed in isolated double wells (Honda et al., PRL 130, 063001, 2023); extended lattices are untested.

topic_review.cite: L. M. Sieberer, M. Buchhold, J. Marino, S. Diehl, Universality in driven open quantum matter, Reviews of Modern Physics, 2025

problems.title: The non-Hermitian skin effect with quantum jumps and interactions
problems.plain: With one-way loss built into a lattice, all waves pile up at one edge, an effect called the skin effect. Whether this survives when real quantum jumps and atom-atom interactions are included is open.
problems.precise: Atoms in a $1\mathrm{D}$ or $2\mathrm{D}$ lattice with engineered nonreciprocal dissipative hopping, evolving under a Lindblad master equation. The effective non-Hermitian Hamiltonian $H_{\mathrm{eff}}$ predicts boundary localization of all modes. Determine whether the full Lindblad dynamics of interacting bosons or fermions shows boundary accumulation with the $H_{\mathrm{eff}}$ length scale, and how quantum jumps and Pauli blocking modify it. Answer: mechanism and measured localization length.
problems.settled_by: An experiment with interacting atoms resolving density profiles under nonreciprocal dissipation, compared with full Lindblad simulation.
problems.status_note: A single-particle skin effect was observed in an atomic momentum-space lattice in 2022 (Liang et al., PRL), and a 2D skin effect in a weakly interacting ultracold Fermi gas was reported in 2025 (Zhao et al., Nature, doi:10.1038/s41586-024-08347-3); interaction and quantum-jump effects remain unmeasured.

topic_review.cite: L. M. Sieberer, M. Buchhold, J. Marino, S. Diehl, Universality in driven open quantum matter, Reviews of Modern Physics, 2025

problems.title: Blackbody radiation shift of lattice clocks at the $10^{-19}$ level
problems.plain: Heat radiation from the room shifts atomic clock frequencies, and for strontium this is one of the largest uncertainties. Controlling it ten times better requires both temperature control and better atomic theory.
problems.precise: Determine the room-temperature (300 K) blackbody shift of the Sr (or Yb) 1S0-3P0 lattice-clock transition, including the dynamic correction from the frequency dependence of the differential polarizability, with fractional uncertainty below $10^{-19}$, and the effective radiation temperature seen by the atoms to 10 mK.
problems.settled_by: Measurement of the differential dynamic polarizability at mid-infrared frequencies combined with in-vacuum thermometry, or cryogenic clock operation that verifies the shift scaling with $T^{4}$ and $T^{6}$.

topic_review.cite: N. Dimarcq et al., Roadmap towards the redefinition of the second, Metrologia, 2024

problems.title: Can optical clocks meet the redefinition criteria by 2029?
problems.plain: Before the second is redefined, several optical clocks around the world must agree, be compared across continents and feed international time routinely. Whether that will be achieved in time for 2030 is not settled.
problems.precise: Determine whether the mandatory criteria of the CCTF roadmap (Dimarcq et al 2024), including repeated agreement of independent optical clocks and frequency ratios at the low-$10^{-18}$ level, continuous contributions to TAI and intercontinental comparisons at that level, are met by 2029 for one species or for an ensemble defining a weighted geometric-mean frequency.
problems.settled_by: BIPM and CCTF assessment confirming each mandatory criterion with published comparison data.
problems.status_note: The 28th CGPM (2026) is to consider the choice of option and species; adoption is expected at the earliest at the 29th CGPM in 2030.

topic_review.cite: N. Dimarcq et al., Roadmap towards the redefinition of the second, Metrologia, 2024

problems.title: Intercontinental optical clock comparison at $10^{-18}$
problems.plain: Clocks on different continents must be compared to check that they agree, but satellite links are not yet good enough. Height differences also matter, since a clock 1 cm higher runs faster by about one part in $10^{18}$.
problems.precise: Achieve a comparison of optical clocks separated by more than 5000 km with total uncertainty below $10^{-18}$, including link noise and the gravitational redshift ($1.1 \times 10^{-18}$ per cm height), which requires geopotential differences known to $10^{3}\,\mathrm{cm}^2\,\mathrm{s}^{-2}$.
problems.settled_by: An intercontinental clock comparison via free-space optical satellite link, transportable clocks or fiber, with an uncertainty budget below $10^{-18}$ and agreement with independent geodesy.

topic_review.cite: N. Dimarcq et al., Roadmap towards the redefinition of the second, Metrologia, 2024

problems.title: What limits the accuracy of a solid-state thorium nuclear clock?
problems.plain: Thorium-229 nuclei embedded in a transparent crystal can be laser-excited, which could make a clock that is compact and insensitive to many disturbances. The crystal environment broadens and shifts the line, and the ultimate accuracy is unknown.
problems.precise: For Th-229 in $\mathrm{CaF_2}$, $\mathrm{LiSrAlF_6}$ or $\mathrm{ThF_4}$ hosts, identify the mechanisms (temperature-dependent electric-field gradients, inhomogeneous broadening from charge-compensating defects, isomer quenching by radiation-induced defects) limiting linewidth and frequency reproducibility, and determine the achievable fractional uncertainty of a solid-state nuclear clock.
problems.settled_by: Repeated measurements across crystals and temperatures with a closed-loop nuclear clock compared to an optical clock, giving a reproducibility budget below $10^{-17}$.
problems.status_note: Temperature sensitivity was measured in 2024, crystal-to-crystal reproducibility in 2025, and a Th-229 nuclear clock with feedback loop was reported in June 2026.

topic_review.cite: N. Dimarcq et al., Roadmap towards the redefinition of the second, Metrologia, 2024

problems.title: Laser excitation of the Th-229 nuclear isomer in a trapped ion
problems.plain: Thorium-229 nuclei have been excited by laser inside crystals, but a single thorium ion held in a trap would avoid crystal disturbances and could make a clock accurate to about one part in $10^{19}$. Laser excitation of the nucleus in a trapped ion has not yet been achieved.
problems.precise: Drive the $8.36\,\mathrm{eV}$ ($148.4\,\mathrm{nm}$) Th-229 isomer transition with a laser in a trapped, sympathetically cooled Th-229 ion (Th3+, whose single valence electron allows laser cooling and state detection, or higher charge states), detect excitation through the hyperfine structure of the electronic transitions, and determine the achievable systematic uncertainty of the resulting clock, predicted to approach $10^{-19}$ (Campbell et al, Physical Review Letters, 2012).
problems.settled_by: Observation of laser-driven isomer excitation in a trapped Th-229 ion, followed by a closed-loop clock operation with an evaluated systematic uncertainty budget.
problems.status_note: Trapped-ion work up to mid-2026 is theoretical or uses isomers populated in the alpha decay of U-233; a 2026 analysis (arXiv 2604.27614) estimates that locating the line in trapped Th3+ takes about one month with existing vacuum-ultraviolet lasers.

topic_review.cite: N. Dimarcq et al., Roadmap towards the redefinition of the second, Metrologia, 2024

problems.title: Does antihydrogen fall with g to within 1 percent?
problems.plain: In 2023 the first direct experiment showed that antihydrogen falls down, not up, but only to about 20% precision. A 1% measurement would test whether antimatter feels gravity exactly like matter.
problems.precise: ALPHA-g measured the vertical acceleration of antihydrogen as $a_g = (0.75 \pm 0.13 stat+sys \pm 0.16 simulation) g$ (2023). Determine $a_g/g$ with total uncertainty below 0.01 and test whether it differs from 1.
problems.settled_by: A laser-cooled antihydrogen release or interferometric measurement (ALPHA-g, GBAR or AEgIS) reaching $1\%$ uncertainty on $a_g$.
problems.status_note: No measurement of $a_g$ more precise than the 2023 ALPHA-g result has been published as of 2026; antihydrogen laser cooling (2021) is the stated prerequisite for the next step.

topic_review.cite: G. M. Tino, L. Cacciapuoti, S. Capozziello, G. Lambiase, F. Sorrentino, Precision gravity tests and the Einstein Equivalence Principle, Progress in Particle and Nuclear Physics, 2020

problems.title: Atom-interferometric test of universality of free fall at $10^{-15}$
problems.plain: Two kinds of atoms dropped together should fall at exactly the same rate. Atom interferometers have checked this to about one part in $10^{12}$, while a satellite with solid masses reached one part in $10^{15}$.
problems.precise: Dual-species atom interferometry (Rb-85/Rb-87, Asenbaum et al 2020) bounds the Eotvos parameter $\eta$ at about $10^{-12}$; MICROSCOPE bounds $\eta(\mathrm{Ti}, \mathrm{Pt})$ at about $10^{-15}$ (2022). Determine $\eta$ for a pair of quantum test masses with uncertainty at or below $10^{-15}$, for example in a $100\,\mathrm{m}$ class tower or in space.
problems.settled_by: A dual-species interferometer result for $\eta$ with total uncertainty below $10^{-15}$ (MAGIS-100, AION, STE-QUEST class).

topic_review.cite: G. M. Tino, L. Cacciapuoti, S. Capozziello, G. Lambiase, F. Sorrentino, Precision gravity tests and the Einstein Equivalence Principle, Progress in Particle and Nuclear Physics, 2020

problems.title: Gravitational time dilation within a single-atom spatial superposition
problems.plain: A clock held higher runs faster, so an atom whose internal ticking is split between two heights at once should carry two different ages that later interfere. This quantum version of gravitational time dilation has been proposed but not measured.
problems.precise: In an atom interferometer whose arms are separated vertically by $\Delta z$ for a time T, with atoms in a superposition of two clock states, general relativity predicts a proper-time difference of order $g\Delta z T/c^{2}$ between the arms, which shifts the clock phase and reduces the clock-state visibility through which-path information (Zych et al 2011; Roura, arXiv 1810.06744). Measure this gravitational proper-time effect, separated from laser-phase and light-shift contributions that cancel in ordinary closed-loop geometries, and determine whether it agrees with the general-relativistic prediction.
problems.settled_by: A clock-state atom interferometer with a verified nonzero gravitational proper-time signal that scales with $\Delta z$ and $T$ as predicted.
problems.status_note: Clock-interferometry schemes, including an optical-tweezer proposal (arXiv 2402.14412, 2024), have been published, but no measurement of a gravitational proper-time difference within a single superposition has been reported as of mid-2026.

topic_review.cite: G. M. Tino, L. Cacciapuoti, S. Capozziello, G. Lambiase, F. Sorrentino, Precision gravity tests and the Einstein Equivalence Principle, Progress in Particle and Nuclear Physics, 2020

links.reason: Both measure time dilation of a clock delocalized in superposition, gravitational or kinematic.

problems.title: Gravitational free fall of muonium or positronium
problems.plain: Muonium (an antimuon with an electron) and positronium (an electron with its antiparticle) contain no protons or neutrons. Measuring how they fall tests gravity on matter made purely of leptons, partly of antimatter.
problems.precise: Measure the gravitational acceleration of muonium (2.2 microsecond lifetime) or long-lived Rydberg positronium with uncertainty below 10% of g, and determine whether it differs from g.
problems.settled_by: A deflection or interferometric measurement of muonium (LEMING) or Rydberg positronium free fall at 10% or better.

topic_review.cite: G. M. Tino, L. Cacciapuoti, S. Capozziello, G. Lambiase, F. Sorrentino, Precision gravity tests and the Einstein Equivalence Principle, Progress in Particle and Nuclear Physics, 2020

problems.title: Do atoms in internal-energy superpositions obey the equivalence principle?
problems.plain: Since energy has mass, an atom in a quantum superposition of two energy levels has no single definite mass. Whether it still falls exactly like a normal atom is a question that classical physics cannot pose.
problems.precise: In the quantum formulation of the equivalence principle (Zych and Brukner, arXiv 1502.00971), the internal mass-energy operator $M = m_0 + H_{\int}/c^2$ may couple to gravity through operators $M_g$ and $M_i$ that differ off-diagonally. Bound the off-diagonal violation parameters for atoms prepared in coherent superpositions of hyperfine or optical clock states at better than $10^{-12}$, improving on the about $10^{-9}$ bound of Rosi et al 2017.
problems.settled_by: An atom interferometer with test atoms in clock-state superpositions measuring the differential acceleration with sub-$10^{-12}$ precision.

topic_review.cite: G. M. Tino, L. Cacciapuoti, S. Capozziello, G. Lambiase, F. Sorrentino, Precision gravity tests and the Einstein Equivalence Principle, Progress in Particle and Nuclear Physics, 2020

problems.title: Universality class of the $Z3$ ordering transition in Rydberg chains
problems.plain: Rydberg chains can order with one excitation every third atom. The transition into this order may belong to an unusual chiral class or pass through an intermediate floating phase.
problems.precise: $1\mathrm{D}$ Rydberg chain with blockade covering two neighbours; the transition from disorder to $\mathrm{Z}3$ order. Determine whether it is direct and chiral (correlation exponent $\nu$ and dynamical exponent $z != 1$), passes through a floating incommensurate phase, or is in the 3-state Potts class at a special point. Answer: phase diagram and exponents along the boundary.
problems.settled_by: Large-scale DMRG with finite-size scaling of the full $1/r^{6}$ Hamiltonian, confirmed by Kibble-Zurek measurements across the boundary.
problems.status_note: Kibble-Zurek data (Keesling et al., Nature 2019) and numerical studies disagree on where the floating phase begins.

topic_review.cite: A. Browaeys, T. Lahaye, Many-body physics with individually controlled Rydberg atoms, Nature Physics, 2020

problems.title: Liquid, glass or crystal in blockaded Rydberg atoms on a kagome lattice
problems.plain: Atoms on a kagome lattice (corner-sharing triangles) that block their neighbours from being excited showed, in early calculations, a disordered region that might be a quantum spin liquid. Later calculations found glassy behaviour or no liquid at all.
problems.precise: H = sum_i (Omega/2) X_i - Delta n_i + sum_i<j (C_6/r_ij^6) n_i n_j on the kagome lattice, in the dense-excitation window between valence-bond-solid phases identified by Samajdar et al. (PNAS 2021). Determine the ground state there: $Z2$ spin liquid, glass-like state from many nearly degenerate solids, or a crystal. Answer: phase identification with topological entanglement entropy or order parameters from large-size numerics.
problems.settled_by: Large-scale quantum Monte Carlo or 2D tensor-network calculations with the full $1/r^{6}$ tails that agree on the phase in this window.
problems.status_note: Samajdar et al. (PNAS 2021, arXiv:2011.12295) found a large-entanglement regime with no local order; Yan et al. (PRL 130, 206501, 2023) found glassy behaviour, and recurrent neural network wave functions found no evidence of a spin liquid (Hibat-Allah et al., Commun. Phys. 2025).

topic_review.cite: A. Browaeys, T. Lahaye, Many-body physics with individually controlled Rydberg atoms, Nature Physics, 2020

problems.title: Is the kagome dipolar XY Rydberg magnet a Dirac spin liquid?
problems.plain: Rydberg atoms can swap excitations with their neighbours, which makes a magnet with competing interactions on a kagome lattice. Calculations predict a spin liquid with massless particle-like excitations, and a 2026 experiment reported a candidate.
problems.precise: Antiferromagnetic dipolar XY model H = J sum_i<j (a/r_ij)^3 (S_i^x S_j^x + S_i^y S_j^y), J > 0, on the kagome lattice, realized by resonant dipolar exchange between Rydberg states. Determine whether the ground state is the gapless $U(1)$ Dirac spin liquid predicted by DMRG (Bintz et al., arXiv:2406.00098), and whether finite arrays reach entropy low enough to distinguish it from a thermal paramagnet. Answer: correlation functions showing power-law decay with exponents matching the Dirac spin liquid (described by quantum electrodynamics in $2+1$ dimensions), or identification of a competing ordered state.
problems.settled_by: Larger-cylinder numerics fixing the ground state, plus measurements on arrays of a few hundred atoms with independent thermometry showing the predicted correlation exponents.
problems.status_note: A 114-atom experiment reported a Dirac spin liquid candidate (Bornet et al., arXiv:2602.14323, 2026), while a 2026 thermometry analysis concluded that further experimental effort is needed to reach the putative spin liquid regime (Fitzner, Lesanovsky, Sbierski, arXiv:2604.22743).

problems.title: Is the Rydberg ruby-lattice spin liquid an equilibrium ground state?
problems.plain: A 2021 experiment saw signs of a quantum spin liquid, a state with hidden long-range quantum entanglement, in atoms on a ruby-shaped lattice. It is unclear whether this was a true lowest-energy state or a product of fast driving.
problems.precise: $H = \sum_i (\Omega/2) X_i - \Delta n_i + \sum_{ij} V_{ij} n_i n_j$ with $V_{ij} = C_6/r_{ij}^6$ on the ruby lattice. Determine whether the ground state at some $(\Delta/\Omega, R_b/a)$ has $Z2$ topological order, diagnosed by topological entanglement entropy $\gamma = \ln 2$ or anyon braiding, with the full $1/r^6$ tails kept. Answer: yes or no with the parameter window.
problems.settled_by: Large-cylinder DMRG or tensor-network calculations with the full interaction showing $\gamma = \ln 2$, matched by an adiabatic preparation that measures anyon statistics.
problems.status_note: Quantum Monte Carlo finds a renormalized classical spin liquid at $T/\Omega = 0.01 \text{ to } 0.5$ in the ruby PXP model, with a shifted entropy plateau once van der Waals tails are kept (Wang and Pollet, arXiv:2406.07110); optimized ramps reach spin-liquid correlations over half the system (Vu et al., PRL 2026, arXiv:2512.09040); ground-state topological order with full $1/r^{6}$ tails is unconfirmed.

topic_review.cite: A. Browaeys, T. Lahaye, Many-body physics with individually controlled Rydberg atoms, Nature Physics, 2020

problems.title: Nature of the striated and star transitions in square Rydberg arrays
problems.plain: On a square grid, Rydberg atoms form several ordered patterns. The transitions into some of them may be smooth or abrupt, and this is not settled.
problems.precise: Square-lattice Rydberg arrays with $R_b/a = 1.2 \text{ to } 1.8$. For transitions from the disordered phase into the striated and star phases, determine whether they are continuous or first order and, if continuous, the universality class (exponents $\nu, \eta$). Answer: classification with exponents.
problems.settled_by: Quantum Monte Carlo or 2D tensor-network finite-size scaling, with Kibble-Zurek scaling on arrays of at least 256 atoms.

problems.title: String-breaking rates in Rydberg lattice gauge theories
problems.plain: A string of field between two charges can snap by creating a new pair of particles, as in the binding of quarks. Rydberg arrays have shown this snapping, and the task is to measure how fast it happens.
problems.precise: For a Rydberg encoding of a (2+1)D $Z2$ or $U(1)$ lattice gauge theory, measure the string-breaking time as a function of string tension $\sigma$ and matter mass $m$, and compare with semiclassical pair-creation rates of the Schwinger form $\Gamma \sim \exp(-c m^2/\sigma)$. Answer: measured scaling and constant $c$ with errors.
problems.settled_by: A systematic scan of $\sigma$ and $m$ on a Rydberg array with breaking times compared to tensor-network or exact simulations.
problems.status_note: String breaking was observed on a (2+1)D Rydberg simulator in 2024 to 2025 (arXiv:2410.16558); quantitative rates and metastability are under study in 2026 (arXiv:2602.22890).

problems.title: Has an analog quench simulation exceeded classical computation?
problems.plain: A 2025 experiment claimed a quantum annealer simulated magnetic dynamics that no supercomputer could match. Classical simulation groups replied with algorithms that may do the same job.
problems.precise: Transverse-field Ising quenches on the square-lattice, dimerized-cubic, diamond-lattice and biclique spin-glass instances of King et al., Science 388, 199 (2025). Determine whether a classical algorithm reproduces the reported correlation functions to the hardware's accuracy with comparable time and energy. Answer: yes or no for each graph family studied.
problems.settled_by: A side-by-side benchmark of classical methods and the device on the same instances with agreed accuracy targets.
problems.status_note: Belief-propagation tensor networks (Tindall et al., Science 2026) and time-dependent variational Monte Carlo (Mauron and Carleo, arXiv:2503.08247) disputed the claim, and a 2026 comment argued neural quantum states are competitive on some instances.

problems.title: Which simulator observables have size-independent error bounds?
problems.plain: Small errors in the controls might add up across many atoms and ruin a big simulation. The question is which measured quantities stay accurate no matter how big the system grows.
problems.precise: Local Hamiltonian $H$ on $N$ sites; the device implements $H+\sum_i \delta h_i$ with $\mid\mid \delta h_i\mid\mid \le \epsilon$. Characterize the classes of states (Gibbs states at temperature T, quench dynamics to time t) and local observables O for which $\left|\langle O\rangle_{\mathrm{device}}-\langle O\rangle_{\mathrm{ideal}}\right|\le f(\epsilon,T,t)$ independent of $N$. Answer: theorems with explicit $f$, and counterexamples outside these classes.
problems.settled_by: Proofs of size-independent bounds for broad classes (for example all gapped ground states or Gibbs states above a threshold temperature) and explicit counterexamples elsewhere.
problems.status_note: 2024 work proved such bounds for some Gibbs states and short-time dynamics (Trivedi, Franco Rubio, Cirac, Nature Communications); ground states and long-time dynamics remain open.

topic_review.cite: A. J. Daley, I. Bloch, C. Kokail, S. Flannigan, N. Pearson, M. Troyer, P. Zoller, Practical quantum advantage in quantum simulation, Nature, 2022

links.reason: Both ask which noisy quantum dynamics keep observables accurate yet classically hard.

problems.title: A classically hard equilibrium observable an analog simulator can reach
problems.plain: Hot quantum systems turn out to be easy for classical computers. The question is whether any cooled simulator can reach a regime that is both hard for classical methods and accessible to the hardware.
problems.precise: Identify a family of local Hamiltonians and a temperature $T$ for which estimating a local observable in the Gibbs state is classically hard (under standard complexity assumptions), while an analog simulator with realistic cooling can prepare that Gibbs state to accuracy $\epsilon$. Answer: an explicit family with a hardness proof and a preparation scheme.
problems.settled_by: A complexity-theoretic hardness proof for a specific Hamiltonian family plus a cooling scheme with proven or measured accuracy.
problems.status_note: 2024 results showed Gibbs states above a constant temperature are efficiently preparable classically (Bakshi, Liu, Moitra, Tang), so any advantage must be at low T.

topic_review.cite: A. J. Daley, I. Bloch, C. Kokail, S. Flannigan, N. Pearson, M. Troyer, P. Zoller, Practical quantum advantage in quantum simulation, Nature, 2022

links.reason: Classically hard Gibbs observables require low-energy states that resist efficient classical sampling.

problems.title: A scalable protocol to certify analog simulator outputs
problems.plain: Checking a simulator by calculation fails exactly where the simulator is useful. The task is a test that needs only modest classical computing and a reasonable number of measurements.
problems.precise: Give a protocol using $\operatorname{poly}(N)$ measurements and $\operatorname{poly}(N)$ classical post-processing (for example Hamiltonian learning, time-reversal echoes, cross-platform comparison of randomized measurements) that bounds the error of local observables of the prepared state relative to the ideal Hamiltonian, for $N > 100$ in a regime where classical simulation is believed hard. Answer: protocol with a proof of soundness and an experimental demonstration.
problems.settled_by: A protocol with a soundness proof applied on hardware with $N > 100$ in a classically hard regime.

links.reason: Both seek efficient classical certification of quantum outputs without trusting the device.

problems.title: Which states produce Feshbach resonances in ultracold atom-molecule collisions?
problems.plain: When ultracold atoms collide with ultracold molecules, the loss rate spikes at certain magnetic fields. Whether these spikes come from loosely bound long-range states or from the tangled short-range states of the three-atom complex is debated.
problems.precise: Collisions of ground-state bialkali molecules with atoms (for example NaK + K, NaLi + Na) show isolated magnetic Feshbach resonances (Yang et al., Science 2019). Determine whether their positions, widths and density arise from long-range states of the atom-molecule pair (Frye and Hutson, Phys. Rev. Research 2023) or from the dense, chaotic short-range spectrum of the triatomic complex. Answer: a model that predicts resonance positions for a new atom-molecule pair before measurement.
problems.settled_by: Advance prediction and subsequent measurement of resonance positions and widths in a previously unmeasured atom-molecule system.
problems.status_note: Frye and Hutson (2023, doi:10.1103/PhysRevResearch.5.023001) attributed observed resonances to long-range states; independent predictive tests are lacking.

topic_review.cite: J. L. Bohn, A. M. Rey, J. Ye, Cold molecules: Progress in quantum engineering of chemistry and quantum matter, Science, 2017

links.reason: Dense atom-molecule resonance spectra test whether chaotic dynamics yields random-matrix statistics.

problems.title: First-principles lifetime of the four-atom collision complex
problems.plain: When two molecules stick, the lifetime of the pair depends on how many internal states it can explore. Calculations of this count disagree with some measurements.
problems.precise: For $(\mathrm{NaK})_2$, $(\mathrm{RbCs})_2$ and $\mathrm{KRb} + \mathrm{KRb}$, compute the sticking lifetime $\tau = 2 \pi \hbar \rho / N_o$, with $\rho$ the density of states of the complex at threshold including conserved total angular momentum, parity and nuclear spin, and $N_o$ the number of open channels. Answer: $\tau$ for each system within a factor 2 of measured values, or a quantified failure of statistical theory.
problems.settled_by: Ab initio density-of-states calculations compared with direct complex-lifetime measurements in light-free traps.

topic_review.cite: J. L. Bohn, A. M. Rey, J. Ye, Cold molecules: Progress in quantum engineering of chemistry and quantum matter, Science, 2017

problems.title: Topological p-wave superfluid of fermionic polar molecules
problems.plain: Fermionic molecules with dipoles, held apart by microwave shields, could pair into a superfluid with a built-in twist (p-wave) that hosts unusual edge states. Current gases are not yet cold enough.
problems.precise: 2D or 3D gas of microwave-shielded fermionic polar molecules (for example NaK) with dipole length $a_{dd}$. Determine the predicted $T_{c}/T_{F}$ for $p_{x} + \mathrm{i} p_{y}$ pairing as a function of $k_{F} a_{dd}$ and shielding parameters, and whether it lies above temperatures reachable by evaporation. Answer: $T_{c}/T_{F}$ with uncertainty and an experimental yes or no.
problems.settled_by: A controlled many-body calculation of $T_{\mathrm{c}}$ including shielding potentials, followed by observation of pairing in a degenerate molecular Fermi gas.
problems.status_note: Evaporation of microwave-shielded NaK reached about $T = 0.36 T_F$ in 2022 (Schindewolf et al., Nature).

topic_review.cite: J. L. Bohn, A. M. Rey, J. Ye, Cold molecules: Progress in quantum engineering of chemistry and quantum matter, Science, 2017

links.reason: Both seek Majorana modes bound to vortices of a p-wave superfluid.

problems.title: Can directly laser-cooled molecules reach quantum degeneracy?
problems.plain: So far every ultracold molecular quantum gas was made by gluing together ultracold atoms. Molecules cooled directly with lasers, which include species useful for precision measurements, have not yet been cooled far enough to behave as a single quantum wave.
problems.precise: Directly laser-cooled molecules (CaF, SrF, YO, CaOH and similar) in optical traps or tweezer-loaded traps. Reach phase-space density $n \lambda_{\mathrm{dB}}^3 \ge 1$ ($\lambda_{\mathrm{dB}}$ the thermal de Broglie wavelength) by evaporative, sympathetic or collisional cooling, which requires a large ratio of elastic to inelastic collisions, for example through microwave or optical shielding. Answer: observation of a Bose-Einstein condensate or degenerate Fermi gas of a laser-cooled species, or a measured collisional obstruction.
problems.settled_by: Bimodal momentum distributions (bosons) or Fermi-surface signatures (fermions) in a gas of directly laser-cooled molecules.
problems.status_note: Blue-detuned magneto-optical traps raised the densities of laser-cooled YO and CaF (Burau et al., PRL 2023; Li et al., PRL 2024), but reported phase-space densities remain far below 1, and a 2025 perspective still describes condensation as a goal (Zeng et al., Quantum Review Letters 2025).

topic_review.cite: J. L. Bohn, A. M. Rey, J. Ye, Cold molecules: Progress in quantum engineering of chemistry and quantum matter, Science, 2017

problems.title: When do ultracold reaction products depart from statistical theory?
problems.plain: A reaction between two ultracold molecules produces new molecules in specific rotation states. Mostly the outcome looks random as statistics predicts, and the exceptions are not understood.
problems.precise: Fully state-resolved reaction $\mathrm{KRb} + \mathrm{KRb} \to \mathrm{K2} + \mathrm{Rb2}$ (and other bialkali reactions). Compare measured product rotational distributions P(N_K2, N_Rb2) with phase-space (statistical) theory and identify the mechanism of any deviations, including nuclear-spin conservation and long-range anisotropic forces. Answer: mechanism with predicted deviations for a second reaction.
problems.settled_by: State-to-state measurements on a second reaction system that confirm a predicted pattern of deviations.
problems.status_note: A 2021 state-to-state study of KRb + KRb found product distributions largely consistent with statistical theory with deviations in some channels (Liu et al., Nature).

topic_review.cite: J. L. Bohn, A. M. Rey, J. Ye, Cold molecules: Progress in quantum engineering of chemistry and quantum matter, Science, 2017

links.reason: Both ask when product distributions depart from statistical phase-space theory.

problems.title: Why do chemically stable ultracold molecules disappear in collisions?
problems.plain: Even molecules that cannot react vanish from traps when they collide. They seem to stick together for a while and are then lost, but the full story is not settled.
problems.precise: Bialkali molecules (RbCs, NaK, NaRb, NaCs) in their absolute ground state with no exothermic reaction channel show two-body loss at near-universal rates. Identify all loss channels of the four-atom complex (trap-light photoexcitation, collisions with a third molecule, other) and account for measured rates quantitatively for each species. Answer: a channel-by-channel budget matching data.
problems.settled_by: Species-by-species measurements of complex lifetimes and loss in light-free traps explained by a single model.
problems.status_note: Photoexcitation by trap light explains loss in several species, but some measured complex lifetimes differ from statistical estimates by large factors (review arXiv:2211.10223).
