problems.title: Which mechanism produced the cosmic baryon asymmetry?
problems.plain: For every billion antiquarks there were about a billion and one quarks in the early universe. Something broke the matter-antimatter balance, and we do not know what.
problems.precise: Explain $\eta_B = n_B/n_\gamma \sim 6.1 \times 10^{-10}$ (CMB and BBN) satisfying the Sakharov conditions, given that SM CP violation and the SM crossover fail by many orders of magnitude. An answer is a mechanism (thermal or resonant leptogenesis, electroweak baryogenesis, Affleck-Dine, or others) with an independent experimental confirmation.
problems.settled_by: Laboratory confirmation of the ingredients of one mechanism, for example lepton number violation plus leptonic CP violation plus heavy neutral leptons for leptogenesis.

topic_review.cite: D. Bodeker, W. Buchmuller, Baryogenesis from the weak scale to the grand unification scale, Reviews of Modern Physics, 2021

links.reason: Antihelium beyond secondary production would require antimatter domains or exotic dark-matter channels.

problems.title: Can electroweak baryogenesis survive the electron EDM bound?
problems.plain: The asymmetry could have formed when the Higgs field switched on, but that needs new CP-violating forces near the weak scale. Such forces would also give the electron a tiny electric dipole, which has not been seen.
problems.precise: Determine whether any model with a strongly first-order electroweak transition and CP violation sufficient for $\eta_B \sim 6 \times 10^{-10}$ is consistent with $\mid d_{e} \mid <$ $4.1 \times 10^{-30}$ e cm (JILA, 2023) and LHC Higgs data. An answer is an explicit viable model with predicted signals, or a general exclusion argument.
problems.settled_by: Next-generation electron EDM measurements (sensitivity $\sim 10^{-31}\,e\,\mathrm{cm}$) combined with Higgs self-coupling and singlet-mixing measurements.
problems.status_note: Most minimal two-Higgs-doublet realizations are excluded by EDMs; models with CP violation in a dark or flavored sector remain.

topic_review.cite: D. Bodeker, W. Buchmuller, Baryogenesis from the weak scale to the grand unification scale, Reviews of Modern Physics, 2021

links.reason: Electron EDM is the leading constraint on electroweak baryogenesis CP violation

problems.title: Do GeV-scale heavy neutral leptons realize low-scale leptogenesis?
problems.plain: In one scenario, heavy partners of neutrinos with masses near a few proton masses created the asymmetry. Such particles could be made at accelerators and seen decaying.
problems.precise: Determine whether heavy neutral leptons N with $M_N \sim 0.1\ \text{to}\ 100\ \mathrm{GeV}$ and active-sterile mixing $U^2$ in the range where resonant or oscillation-based (ARS) leptogenesis gives $\eta_B \sim 6 \times 10^{-10}$ exist. An answer is a discovery with measured $M_N$, $U_e^2$, $U_{\mu}^2$, $U_{\tau}^2$ consistent with that region, or its exclusion.
problems.settled_by: Beam-dump and collider searches (SHiP, displaced-vertex searches at LHC, FCC-ee at the Z pole) covering the leptogenesis region.
problems.status_note: SHiP was approved at CERN in 2024 for operation in the 2030s.

topic_review.cite: D. Bodeker, W. Buchmuller, Baryogenesis from the weak scale to the grand unification scale, Reviews of Modern Physics, 2021

problems.title: Can DAMA's background subtraction create a spurious yearly modulation?
problems.plain: DAMA subtracts each year's average rate before looking for a yearly wave; if the true rate drifts slowly, this step can manufacture a wave that is not there. The question is whether this explains all or part of the signal.
problems.precise: DAMA forms residuals by subtracting the annual mean rate per energy bin, cycle by cycle (roughly September to September). For a time-dependent background $B(t)$ (e.g., decaying cosmogenic or radiogenic components, or slow gain drift), this procedure induces a sawtooth residual whose fit to $A$ $\mathrm{cos}(2 \pi (t - t0)/1\,\mathrm{yr})$ can give a nonzero A with a phase that depends on $\mathrm{d}B/\mathrm{d}t$. An answer is a quantitative yes or no: whether a background evolution consistent with DAMA's published spectra and stability data reproduces the reported amplitude and phase.
problems.settled_by: Analysis of DAMA's absolute, non-subtracted single-hit rate versus time per energy bin, or a full forward model of the DAMA background evolution fitted to their data.
problems.status_note: Buttazzo, Panci, Rossi and Strumia (JHEP 2020) showed the mechanism can produce a modulation, and COSINE-100 (Sci. Rep. 2023) showed that applying the DAMA method to COSINE-100 data induces an artificial modulation; DAMA and Messina, Nardecchia and Piacentini (JCAP 2020) dispute that it applies to DAMA data.

topic_review.cite: N. Carlin et al. (COSINE-100 and ANAIS-112 Collaborations), Combined Annual Modulation Dark Matter Search with COSINE-100 and ANAIS-112, Phys. Rev. Lett. 135, 121002, 2025

problems.title: Does crystal-specific NaI(Tl) response hide a DAMA-only signal?
problems.plain: Sodium iodide crystals turn the energy of a recoiling sodium nucleus into light with an efficiency (the quenching factor) that can differ between crystals. If DAMA's crystals differ from the others, a real signal might show up only in DAMA.
problems.precise: The sodium recoil quenching factor $Q_{\mathrm{Na}}(E_{R})$ in NaI(Tl) converts nuclear recoil energy to electron-equivalent energy and has been measured between roughly 0.1 and 0.3 for $E_{R} \sim 10-100\, \mathrm{keV}$, with dependence on thallium concentration. The question is the value of $Q_{\mathrm{Na}}(E_{R})$ and of the near-threshold light yield for DAMA's own crystals, and whether any value within that range brings the DAMA modulation into agreement with COSINE-100 and ANAIS-112 when compared at equal nuclear recoil energy rather than equal electron-equivalent energy.
problems.settled_by: A direct neutron-beam quenching-factor measurement on a DAMA-equivalent crystal (same supplier, Tl concentration and growth), followed by a recoil-energy-matched comparison of the three experiments.
problems.status_note: COSINUS (Eur. Phys. J. C 2026, arXiv 2512.05980) measured that lower Tl concentration gives a smaller Na quenching factor, confirming crystal dependence.

topic_review.cite: N. Carlin et al. (COSINE-100 and ANAIS-112 Collaborations), Combined Annual Modulation Dark Matter Search with COSINE-100 and ANAIS-112, Phys. Rev. Lett. 135, 121002, 2025

problems.title: Are DAMA-region NaI events nuclear or electron recoils?
problems.plain: A dark matter particle would mostly knock a nucleus, while radioactivity mostly knocks electrons. A cooled sodium iodide detector that measures both heat and light can tell these apart.
problems.precise: Conventional NaI(Tl) scintillators cannot discriminate nuclear from electron recoils at 1-6 keVee. A cryogenic NaI scintillating calorimeter (COSINUS at LNGS) reads phonon and scintillation channels, giving recoil-type discrimination event by event. The question is the composition of the 1-6 keVee rate in NaI and whether any modulating component is nuclear-recoil-like.
problems.settled_by: A COSINUS-type measurement with nuclear-electron recoil discrimination and enough exposure to test the DAMA rate and modulation in the nuclear-recoil band.
problems.status_note: COSINUS-1pi Run 1 with eight cryogenic NaI modules at LNGS was planned to start data taking in 2026 (Commun. Phys. 9, 213, 2026); no result yet.

topic_review.cite: N. Carlin et al. (COSINE-100 and ANAIS-112 Collaborations), Combined Annual Modulation Dark Matter Search with COSINE-100 and ANAIS-112, Phys. Rev. Lett. 135, 121002, 2025

problems.title: What produces the DAMA/LIBRA annual modulation?
problems.plain: DAMA/LIBRA sees a yearly rise and fall in low-energy events, peaking in late May or early June, but identical-material experiments see nothing. The question is what physical or instrumental effect makes the DAMA rate oscillate.
problems.precise: DAMA/NaI plus DAMA/LIBRA phases 1 and 2 report a single-hit residual rate in NaI(Tl) with amplitude about 0.01 cpd/kg/keV in 2-6 keV electron-equivalent energy (phase 2 alone extends this to 1-6 keV), period 1 yr and phase in late May, consistent within errors with the June 2 dark matter expectation, at $13.7\sigma$ for 2.86 t yr (2021) and $15.3\sigma$ for 3.40 t yr (2026). COSINE-100 and ANAIS-112, with the same target, find amplitudes consistent with zero. An answer identifies the source of the DAMA modulation (dark matter with crystal-specific response, an environmental or detector effect, or an analysis artifact) and demonstrates it quantitatively on DAMA data or an equivalent setup.
problems.settled_by: Reproduction or elimination of the modulation in a NaI(Tl) setup that matches DAMA's crystals, energy calibration and analysis, together with release and independent analysis of DAMA's absolute rate time series.
problems.status_note: In 2025 COSINE-100 and ANAIS-112 combined 3-year data gave amplitudes $-0.0002 \pm 0.0026$ $\left(1-6\,\mathrm{keV}\right)$ and $0.0021 \pm 0.0028\,\mathrm{cpd}/\mathrm{kg}/\mathrm{keV}$ $\left(2-6\,\mathrm{keV}\right)$, and their 6-year data gave $0.0005 \pm 0.0019$ and $0.0027 \pm 0.0021$, excluding DAMA at $4.7\ \text{and}\ 3.5\,\sigma$; DAMA reported $15.3\,\sigma$ in $2-6\,\mathrm{keV}$ with $3.40\,\mathrm{t}\,\mathrm{yr}$ in 2026 (Nucl. Phys. At. Energy 27, 2026) and identifies no systematic.

topic_review.cite: N. Carlin et al. (COSINE-100 and ANAIS-112 Collaborations), Combined Annual Modulation Dark Matter Search with COSINE-100 and ANAIS-112, Phys. Rev. Lett. 135, 121002, 2025

problems.title: Does a Southern Hemisphere NaI detector see the same-phase modulation?
problems.plain: Seasons are reversed in the Southern Hemisphere, but Earth's motion through dark matter is not. A sodium iodide detector in Australia tests whether DAMA's yearly wave follows the seasons or the dark matter.
problems.precise: SABRE South (Stawell Underground Physics Laboratory, Australia, about 2900 m water equivalent) operates low-background NaI(Tl) crystals with a liquid scintillator veto. The question is whether its 1-6 keV single-hit rate shows a modulation with amplitude near 0.01 cpd/kg/keV and phase near June 2 (dark matter like), phase shifted by about six months (seasonal environment like), or no modulation.
problems.settled_by: A multi-year SABRE South modulation analysis with sensitivity to exclude or confirm the DAMA amplitude at $3\sigma$ or better, ideally with its twin SABRE North at LNGS.
problems.status_note: SABRE South completed underground assembly milestones in 2025 with full commissioning planned for 2026.

topic_review.cite: N. Carlin et al. (COSINE-100 and ANAIS-112 Collaborations), Combined Annual Modulation Dark Matter Search with COSINE-100 and ANAIS-112, Phys. Rev. Lett. 135, 121002, 2025

problems.title: Why do e+e- to pi+ pi- cross-section measurements disagree?
problems.plain: Measurements of how often electron-positron collisions make two pions disagree between experiments, and with supercomputer calculations. This number feeds the muon magnet prediction.
problems.precise: Identify the cause of the disagreement among $\sigma(e+e- \to \pi+ \pi-)$ measurements near the $\rho$ peak (CMD-3 2023 versus KLOE, BaBar, SND) and between data-driven and lattice a_mu^HVP,LO (difference $\sim 2\ \text{to}\ 3\%$ of HVP). An answer locates the systematic error, the radiative-correction issue, or a physical effect responsible.
problems.settled_by: New $\pi\,\pi$ measurements (BaBar reanalysis, Belle II, BESIII, KLOE reanalysis, CMD-3 crosscheck) together with lattice windows and $\tau$-decay data with isospin-breaking corrections.
problems.status_note: Unresolved as of 2025; the 2025 White Paper did not use data-driven HVP for its central value.

topic_review.cite: R. Aliberti et al., The anomalous magnetic moment of the muon in the Standard Model: an update, Physics Reports, 2025

problems.title: Does the SM match the final muon g-2 measurement?
problems.plain: The muon behaves like a tiny magnet whose strength was measured to about one part in ten million. The SM prediction now agrees, but only after replacing one method of computing the strong-force part with another.
problems.precise: Fermilab's final result (2025) gives $a_{\mu} = 116592070.5(14.8) x 1e-11\ (127\ \mathrm{ppb})$; the world average with BNL is $116592071.5(14.5) x 1e-11\ (124\ \mathrm{ppb})$; the 2025 Theory Initiative prediction using lattice-QCD HVP (hadronic vacuum polarization) is $116592033(62) x 1e-11$, in agreement. The residual question is whether the SM prediction with uncertainty $\sim 20 \times 1e-11$ still agrees once data-driven and lattice HVP are reconciled.
problems.settled_by: Lattice HVP at $\sim 0.2\%$ from several groups, consistent $e+e-$ hadronic data, the MUonE spacelike HVP measurement, and the J-PARC muon $g-2$ experiment.
problems.status_note: In 2025 the long-standing $4\ \text{to}\ 5\,\sigma$ discrepancy disappeared with the lattice-based SM value; the data-driven value remains inconsistent.

topic_review.cite: R. Aliberti et al., The anomalous magnetic moment of the muon in the Standard Model: an update, Physics Reports, 2025

problems.title: Is there a new scalar boson near 95 GeV?
problems.plain: Searches for extra Higgs-like particles at the LHC, and earlier at the LEP collider, show small excesses of events near 95 GeV, below the known 125 GeV Higgs. Each excess is weak by itself, and it is unknown whether they come from one real particle.
problems.precise: Run 2 diphoton searches show excesses near $m = 95.4 \mathrm{GeV}$ in CMS ($2.9\sigma$ local) and ATLAS ($1.7\sigma$ local), about $3.1\sigma$ local combined (Biekotter, Heinemeyer, Weiglein, arXiv:2306.03889); CMS also reported a ditau excess of $2.6 \text{ to } 3.1\sigma$ local at 95 to 100 GeV, and LEP a mild bb excess near 98 GeV. Determine whether a scalar S with $m_{S} \sim 95 \mathrm{GeV}$ exists, by a $\ge 5\sigma$ observation in at least one channel or exclusion of the production rates needed to fit the excesses.
problems.settled_by: LHC Run 3 and HL-LHC low-mass diphoton, ditau and bb searches, and a recoil-mass search for $e+ e- \to Z S$ at a Higgs factory.
problems.status_note: Phenomenology papers through mid-2026 still quote a combined diphoton excess near $3\sigma$ local; no Run 3 result confirming or removing it was found in this review (moderate confidence).

topic_review.cite: R. Aliberti et al., The anomalous magnetic moment of the muon in the Standard Model: an update, Physics Reports, 2025

problems.title: What explains the CDF W mass measurement disagreement?
problems.plain: In 2022 the CDF experiment reported a W boson mass well above the SM prediction. Later measurements at the LHC agree with the SM, leaving the CDF result unexplained.
problems.precise: CDF (2022) measured $m_{W} = 80433.5 \pm 9.4\,\mathrm{MeV}$, about $7\,\sigma$ above the electroweak fit $80357 \pm 6\,\mathrm{MeV}$; ATLAS (2024, $80366.5 \pm 15.9\,\mathrm{MeV}$) and CMS (2024, $80360.2 \pm 9.9\,\mathrm{MeV}$) agree with the SM. Identify the source of the CDF discrepancy (PDF, recoil modeling, detector calibration) or show it reflects new physics.
problems.settled_by: A joint Tevatron-LHC reanalysis with common PDFs and modeling, plus further LHC and future $e+e-$ threshold measurements of $m_W$.
problems.status_note: After the 2024 CMS result the SM value is favored; the CDF disagreement has no accepted explanation.

topic_review.cite: R. Aliberti et al., The anomalous magnetic moment of the muon in the Standard Model: an update, Physics Reports, 2025

problems.title: Is the Belle II $B\,\mathrm{to}\,K\,\nu\,\nu$ excess real?
problems.plain: Belle II found that B mesons decay to a kaon plus invisible particles more often than expected, about four times the predicted rate. It could be new particles or a fluctuation.
problems.precise: Belle II (2023) measured BR(B+ -> K+ nu nubar) = (2.3 +- 0.7) x $10^{-5}$, $2.7\,\sigma$ above the SM prediction ($\sim 0.5 \times 1e-5$). Determine whether the excess persists at $\ge 5\,\sigma$ and whether it shows a peak in invisible mass from a new light particle.
problems.settled_by: Belle II with about 5 to 10 $\mathrm{ab}^{-1}$ and NA62-style rare kaon decays for related b to s and s to d invisible channels.
problems.status_note: The $2.7\sigma$ excess is still the latest measurement as of 2026.

topic_review.cite: HFLAV Collaboration, Averages of b-hadron, c-hadron, and tau-lepton properties as of 2023, Physical Review D, 2026

problems.title: Are $b \text{ to } s \mu \mu$ tensions new physics or charm-loop effects?
problems.plain: After a well-known hint was withdrawn in 2022, some B decays to muon pairs still occur less often, or with different angular patterns, than predicted. Whether hard-to-compute strong-force effects explain this is disputed.
problems.precise: Branching ratios of $B \to K \mu \mu$ and $B_{s} \to \phi \mu \mu$ at low $q^{2}$ and the angular observable $P5'$ in $B \to K* \mu \mu$ deviate from SM predictions by about $2 \text{ to } 4 \sigma$, while $R_{K}$ and $R_{K}*$ agree with the SM (LHCb, 2022). Identify whether a shift in the Wilson coefficient $C_{9}$ is short-distance new physics or long-distance c-cbar loops.
problems.settled_by: Data-driven determination of the $q^{2}$ dependence of non-local charm contributions from LHCb Run 3 and Belle II, combined with lattice form factors.

topic_review.cite: HFLAV Collaboration, Averages of b-hadron, c-hadron, and tau-lepton properties as of 2023, Physical Review D, 2026

problems.title: Is first-row CKM unitarity violated (Cabibbo angle anomaly)?
problems.plain: The probabilities for an up quark to turn into each kind of down-type quark should add to exactly one. Current data fall short by about a tenth of a percent, roughly 3 standard deviations.
problems.precise: Test $\left|V_{ud}\right|^2 + \left|V_{us}\right|^2 + \left|V_{ub}\right|^2 = 1$, with $V_{ud}$ from superallowed $0+$ to $0+$ nuclear beta decays and neutron decay, and $V_{us}$ from K_l3, K_mu2/pi_mu2 and $\tau$ decays. The current deficit is of order $10^{-3}$ at about $3\sigma$, together with an internal K_l3 versus K_mu2 tension; an answer is confirmation above $5\sigma$ or resolution to below $2\sigma$.
problems.settled_by: Improved electroweak radiative corrections and nuclear-structure corrections for superallowed decays, new lattice QCD form factors for K_l3, and new K_l3/K_mu2 ratio measurements (NA62).
problems.status_note: A 2026 lattice-QCD analysis (arXiv:2604.04715) and related work still find a first-row deficit near $3\sigma$.

problems.title: Is lepton flavor universality violated in $b\,\mathrm{to}\,c\,\tau\,\nu$ decays?
problems.plain: The SM treats electrons, muons and taus alike except for mass. B meson decays to $\tau$ leptons occur more often than predicted, by more than 3 standard deviations.
problems.precise: Determine whether $R(D)=\operatorname{BR}(B \to D \tau \nu)/\operatorname{BR}(B \to D \ell \nu)$ and $R(D*)$ exceed the SM values (HFLAV arithmetic average of predictions $0.296 \pm 0.004\ \text{and}\ 0.254 \pm 0.005$). The HFLAV ICHEP 2026 averages are $R(D)=0.359 \pm 0.024$ and $R(D*) = 0.280 \pm 0.011$ (correlation -0.37), about $3.7\,\sigma$ above the SM combined; an answer is $\ge 5\,\sigma$ confirmation or reduction below $2\,\sigma$.
problems.settled_by: Belle II with several $\mathrm{ab}^{-1}$ and LHCb Run 3 measurements using hadronic and leptonic $\tau$ decays, with lattice form factors for $B \to D*$.
problems.status_note: The HFLAV average updated for ICHEP 2026 (August 2026, including a new Belle II $R(D*)$ result) gives about $3.7\sigma$.

topic_review.cite: HFLAV Collaboration, Averages of b-hadron, c-hadron, and tau-lepton properties as of 2023, Physical Review D, 2026

problems.title: Does muon-to-electron conversion occur at rates near $10^{-16}$?
problems.plain: The SM forbids a muon from turning into an electron without neutrinos, except at hopelessly tiny rates. Seeing it would prove new physics acting on flavor.
problems.precise: Measure or bound the coherent conversion rate $R_{\mathrm{mue}} = \Gamma(\mu- N \to e- N)/\Gamma(\mu- \mathrm{capture})$ on aluminum at single-event sensitivity $\sim 10^{-17}$ (Mu2e, COMET), versus the SINDRUM II gold limit of about $7 \times 10^{-13}$. Combine with $\mu \to e\gamma$ (MEG II) and $\mu \to 3e$ (Mu3e) to identify the operator responsible if seen.
problems.settled_by: Mu2e at Fermilab and COMET at J-PARC reaching single-event sensitivity near $10^{-17}$.
problems.status_note: MEG II reported $\mathrm{BR}(\mu \to e \gamma) < \sim 1.5 \times 10^{-13}$ in 2025 (moderate confidence on the exact value); Mu2e and COMET are expected to start physics running around 2027.

topic_review.cite: F. Feruglio, Pieces of the flavour puzzle, European Physical Journal C, 2015

problems.title: Why are there exactly three fermion generations?
problems.plain: Experiments show three light neutrino types and three sets of quarks and leptons, and a fourth ordinary copy is ruled out. Why three, and not one or four, is unknown.
problems.precise: LEP Z-width data give $N_\nu = 2.9963 \pm 0.0074$ light neutrino species after the 2020 luminosity correction (Janot and Jadach), and Higgs production rates exclude a fourth sequential chiral generation. An answer is a principle (anomaly cancellation in an extended gauge group, string compactification topology, or a symmetry argument) that requires $N_{\mathrm{g}} = 3$ and makes a further testable prediction.
problems.settled_by: A framework deriving $N_g = 3$ whose additional predictions are verified experimentally.

topic_review.cite: F. Feruglio, Pieces of the flavour puzzle, European Physical Journal C, 2015

problems.title: What determines the hierarchy of quark and lepton masses?
problems.plain: The top quark is about 340000 times heavier than the electron, and quark mixing is small while neutrino mixing is large. No theory predicts these numbers.
problems.precise: The SM Yukawa couplings span $y_e \sim 3 \times 10^{-6}$ to $y_t \sim 1$, CKM angles are small ($\theta_C \sim 0.23$, $\mid V_{ub}\mid$ $\sim 4 \times 10^{-3}$) while PMNS angles are large ($\theta_{12} \sim 34\,\mathrm{deg}$, $\theta_{23} \sim 45\,\mathrm{deg}$). An answer is a mechanism (Froggatt-Nielsen charges, modular or discrete flavor symmetries, extra-dimensional localization, partial compositeness) that predicts these values with fewer parameters than it explains.
problems.settled_by: A model with fewer free parameters than observables whose extra predictions (mixing sum rules, flavor-violating rates, new states) are confirmed.

topic_review.cite: F. Feruglio, Pieces of the flavour puzzle, European Physical Journal C, 2015

problems.title: Do the SM gauge forces unify into a single group?
problems.plain: The strengths of the three forces change with energy and nearly meet near $10^{16}\, \mathrm{GeV}$. Whether they truly become one force is unknown.
problems.precise: Determine whether SU(3) x SU(2) x U(1) embeds in a simple group ($\mathrm{SU}(5), \mathrm{SO}(10), \mathrm{E6}$) broken near $M_{\mathrm{GUT}} \sim 10^{15}\ \text{to}\ 10^{16}\,\mathrm{GeV}$. In the SM the three couplings do not meet at a point; in the MSSM they meet at $\sim 2 \times 10^{16}\,\mathrm{GeV}$. An answer is an observation of a unification-specific effect such as proton decay with a branching pattern fixed by the group.
problems.settled_by: Detection of proton decay in one or more channels with branching ratios matching a specific GUT.

topic_review.cite: P. Nath, P. Fileviez Perez, Proton stability in grand unified theories, in strings and in branes, Physics Reports, 2007

problems.title: Do neutrons oscillate into antineutrons?
problems.plain: Some theories allow a neutron to turn into its own antiparticle, changing baryon number by two. This would not show up in proton decay searches.
problems.precise: Search for $\Delta B = 2$ neutron-antineutron oscillations with free-neutron oscillation time $\tau_{\mathrm{nnbar}} > 8.6 \times 10^{7}\,\mathrm{s}$ (ILL, 1994) and bound-neutron limits converting to $\sim 4.7 \times 10^{8}\,\mathrm{s}$ (Super-Kamiokande, 2021). An answer is a detection or a free-neutron limit improved by 1 to 3 orders of magnitude.
problems.settled_by: The proposed NNBAR experiment at the European Spallation Source and bound-neutron searches in DUNE and Hyper-Kamiokande.

problems.title: Does the proton decay to an antineutrino and a kaon?
problems.plain: Supersymmetric unified theories favor a different decay of the proton, into an antineutrino and a charged kaon. Detecting the kaon needs detectors with good tracking.
problems.precise: Measure or bound $\tau(p \to \mathrm{anti}-\nu K+)/B$, currently $> \sim 5.9 \times 10^{33}\,\mathrm{yr}$ (Super-Kamiokande, 2014). Minimal SUSY $\mathrm{SU}(5)$ with dimension-5 operators predicts values near or below this; an answer is a detection or a limit $\sim 10^{34}\text{ to }10^{35}\,\mathrm{yr}$.
problems.settled_by: DUNE liquid-argon tracking, Hyper-Kamiokande and JUNO searches for p -> anti-nu K+.

topic_review.cite: P. Nath, P. Fileviez Perez, Proton stability in grand unified theories, in strings and in branes, Physics Reports, 2007

problems.title: Is the proton lifetime to $e+ \pi0$ below $10^{35}\,\mathrm{years}$?
problems.plain: Grand unified theories predict a proton can decay into a positron and a neutral pion. Huge water detectors watch for this rare event.
problems.precise: Measure or bound $\tau(p \to e+ \pi0)/B$, currently $> 2.4 \times 10^{34}\,\mathrm{yr}$ (Super-Kamiokande, 2020, 90 percent CL). Non-supersymmetric $\mathrm{SO}(10)$ models with intermediate scales typically predict $10^{34}\text{ to }10^{36}\,\mathrm{yr}$. An answer is a detection or a limit near $10^{35}\,\mathrm{yr}$.
problems.settled_by: Hyper-Kamiokande exposure of about 1 to 2 Mt-yr reaching $\sim 10^{35}\,\mathrm{yr}$ sensitivity.
problems.status_note: Hyper-Kamiokande construction is under way, with data expected late in the 2020s.

topic_review.cite: P. Nath, P. Fileviez Perez, Proton stability in grand unified theories, in strings and in branes, Physics Reports, 2007

problems.title: Is the weak scale set by cosmological dynamics or selection?
problems.plain: Instead of new particles at the TeV scale, the Higgs mass might have been adjusted during the early universe by a slowly evolving field, or selected among many possible universes. Such ideas predict light, weakly coupled particles instead of heavy ones.
problems.precise: Assess mechanisms in which v is fixed dynamically by cosmological evolution (relaxion scanning of $m_h^{2}$, NNaturalness, crunching of regions with large v) rather than by TeV-scale symmetry. An answer is a consistent model that reproduces $v = 246\,\mathrm{GeV}$ without large tuning and an experimental signature (for example relaxion-Higgs mixing or fifth forces) that can confirm or exclude it.
problems.settled_by: Detection or exclusion of the light scalar predicted by relaxation models through Higgs-mixing searches, fifth-force tests and rare-decay searches across its allowed mass range.
problems.status_note: Relaxion proposals date from 2015; consistent models exist but require long inflation or other non-minimal features, and none has a confirmed signature.

topic_review.cite: G. F. Giudice, The Dawn of the Post-Naturalness Era, arXiv, 2017

links.reason: Selection or relaxation mechanisms are proposed for both small scales together.

problems.title: Is the Higgs boson elementary or a composite bound state?
problems.plain: The Higgs could be a point-like particle or a bound state of new strongly interacting constituents, much as a pion is made of quarks. A composite Higgs would show small deviations in how it couples to other particles.
problems.precise: In composite pseudo-Goldstone Higgs models, Higgs couplings to W, Z and fermions deviate from SM values by $\mid \kappa - 1 \mid \sim \xi = v^{2}/f^{2}$ up to $O(1)$ factors, with f the compositeness scale. Determine whether $\xi > 0$ by measuring $\kappa_V$ and $\kappa_f$ to 0.1 to 1 percent, or find the associated resonances of mass $m_\rho \sim g_\rho f$ with $1 < g_\rho < 4\pi$.
problems.settled_by: Higgs coupling measurements at a Higgs factory (FCC-ee, CEPC or a linear collider) at the per-mille level for $\kappa_Z$, combined with high-energy searches for resonances.
problems.status_note: LHC coupling fits (2024 to 2025) agree with the SM at about the 5 to 10 percent level, implying $\xi < \sim 0.1$ and $f > \sim 0.8\,\mathrm{TeV}$.

topic_review.cite: G. F. Giudice, The Dawn of the Post-Naturalness Era, arXiv, 2017

links.reason: Composite Higgs models need gauge theories near the lower conformal-window edge.

problems.title: Do color-neutral top partners, as in Twin Higgs models, exist?
problems.plain: Some proposals keep the Higgs light with partner particles that do not feel the strong force, so the LHC barely produces them. They would show up as small shifts in Higgs couplings, or as Higgs decays to hidden-sector particles that fly a measurable distance before decaying.
problems.precise: In neutral-naturalness models (Twin Higgs, folded supersymmetry, quirky little Higgs) the top-loop contribution to $m_h^{2}$ is cancelled by states without SM color, with a mirror-sector scale f; Higgs couplings shift by about $v^{2}/(2 f^{2})$ and the Higgs can decay to mirror glueballs with displaced vertices (approximate relations, model dependent). Determine whether such a sector exists with $f\ \text{below about}\ 1\ \text{to}\ 2\ \mathrm{TeV}$, by measuring $\mathrm{BR}(h \to \text{mirror hadrons})$ down to about $10^{-4}$ and Higgs couplings at the per-mille level, or exclude it.
problems.settled_by: Displaced-vertex searches for exotic Higgs decays at the HL-LHC and at dedicated long-lived-particle detectors, together with per-mille Higgs coupling measurements at a Higgs factory.
problems.status_note: No exotic Higgs decays to long-lived particles observed through LHC Run 2; Batell, Low, Neil and Verhaaren review the open parameter space (Physics Reports 1165, 2026, arXiv:2203.05531).

topic_review.cite: G. F. Giudice, The Dawn of the Post-Naturalness Era, arXiv, 2017

problems.title: Why is the electroweak scale so far below the Planck scale?
problems.plain: The Higgs field sets the masses of most particles at about $246\,\mathrm{GeV}$, roughly $10^{17}$ times below the scale where gravity becomes strong. No known principle explains this huge gap without extreme fine cancellations.
problems.precise: In the SM with a cutoff $\Lambda$, the top loop gives $\delta m_h^{2} \sim -(3 y_t^{2}/(8 \pi^{2})) \Lambda^{2}$, so $m_h = 125\,\mathrm{GeV}$ with $\Lambda \sim M_{\mathrm{Pl}} \sim 1.2 \times 10^{19}\,\mathrm{GeV}$ requires cancellation to about 1 part in $10^{33}$. An answer is a mechanism (symmetry, compositeness, dynamics or selection) that yields $v = 246\,\mathrm{GeV}$ with at most mild tuning and is consistent with all LHC data.
problems.settled_by: Discovery at a collider of the particles or form factors predicted by a specific mechanism, or a calculable non-collider mechanism confirmed by its own distinct predictions.
problems.status_note: LHC Run 2 and early Run 3 data (to 2025) show no top partners, superpartners or composite resonances near 1 TeV, pushing simple natural models to percent-level tuning or worse.

topic_review.cite: G. F. Giudice, The Dawn of the Post-Naturalness Era, arXiv, 2017

problems.title: Do colored top partners exist below a few TeV?
problems.plain: Most proposed fixes for the light Higgs predict a heavy cousin of the top quark (a top partner) that cancels the top quark's large push on the Higgs mass. If such particles exist, they should appear at colliders with masses not far above 1 TeV.
problems.precise: Determine whether colored states that cancel the top-loop contribution to $m_h^2$ (scalar stops in supersymmetry, vector-like fermionic top partners in composite-Higgs models) exist with mass $m_T < \sim 3\ \mathrm{TeV}$. Current LHC 13 TeV limits exclude stops up to about 1.2 to 1.3 TeV for a light neutralino and vector-like top partners up to roughly 1.5 TeV (approximate, model dependent).
problems.settled_by: Direct searches at the high-luminosity LHC ($3000\,\mathrm{fb}^{-1}$) and a future $100\,\mathrm{TeV}$ hadron collider covering pair production up to $m_T \sim 2\,\mathrm{TeV}$ and $\sim 10\,\mathrm{TeV}$ respectively.
problems.status_note: No signal through LHC Run 2; Run 3 at 13.6 TeV ongoing in 2026.

topic_review.cite: G. F. Giudice, The Dawn of the Post-Naturalness Era, arXiv, 2017

problems.title: Does the Higgs field give the electron its mass?
problems.plain: The electron couples to the Higgs so weakly (strength about 3 in a million) that the coupling has never been detected. Measuring it would show whether the Higgs field is the source of the mass of the particle that sets the size of atoms.
problems.precise: Measure the electron Yukawa coupling $y_e$ (SM value $\sqrt{2}\,m_e/v \sim 2.9 \times 10^{-6}$), or $\kappa_e = y_e/y_e^{\mathrm{SM}}$. The best direct bound, CMS $\operatorname{BR}(H \to e+ e-) < 3.0 \times 10^{-4}$ at 95 percent CL (Phys. Lett. B 846, 137783, 2023), corresponds to $\left|\kappa_e\right| < \sim 240$ (approximate, using $\operatorname{BR}_{\mathrm{SM}} \sim 5 \times 10^{-9}$). An answer is $\kappa_e$ measured with $O(1)$ precision, enough to separate $\kappa_e = 1$ from $\kappa_e = 0$.
problems.settled_by: Resonant s-channel production $e+ e- \to H$ at $\sqrt{s}=m_{H}$ with a center-of-mass energy spread of about 4 MeV at FCC-ee, projected to reach $1.3\,\sigma$ for the SM coupling (an upper limit of 1.6 times $y_{e}^{\mathrm{SM}}$) per interaction point per year with $10\,\mathrm{ab}^{-1}$ (d'Enterria, Poldaru, Wojcik, Eur. Phys. J. Plus 137, 201, 2022, arXiv:2107.02686).
problems.status_note: Only upper bounds exist as of 2026; FCC-ee feasibility studies reach sensitivity near the SM value.

topic_review.cite: ATLAS Collaboration, Characterising the Higgs boson with ATLAS data from Run 2 of the LHC, Physics Reports, 2025

problems.title: Do the muon and charm quark couple to the Higgs with SM strength?
problems.plain: The Higgs has been seen decaying to the heavy third-generation fermions, but its decays to the muon and to the charm quark (second-generation particles) are rare and only hinted at. Confirming them would show that the Higgs gives mass the same way across generations.
problems.precise: Measure the coupling modifiers $\kappa_{\mu}$ and $\kappa_c$ relative to the SM. ATLAS Run 2 plus Run 3 $H \to \mu\mu$ gives $3.4\sigma$ ($2.5\sigma$ expected) with signal strength $1.4 \pm 0.4$ (Phys. Rev. Lett. 135, 231802, 2025), CMS Run 2 gives $3.0\sigma$; the best direct charm bound is $\left|\kappa_c\right| < 4.2$ at 95 percent CL (ATLAS VH, JHEP 04 (2025) 075). An answer is a $\ge 5\sigma$ observation of $H \to \mu\mu$ with $\kappa_{\mu}$ to $\sim 10\%$, and a $\kappa_c$ measurement that separates 1 from 0.
problems.settled_by: HL-LHC $H \to \mu \mu$ and $H \to c\ \mathrm{cbar}$ analyses, followed by percent-level $\mathrm{BR}(H \to c\ \mathrm{cbar})$ and $\operatorname{BR}(H \to \mu \mu)$ measurements at a Higgs factory.
problems.status_note: Evidence-level $H \to \mu\mu$ from ATLAS (2025) and CMS (2020); $H \to c\,\mathrm{cbar}$ not observed, with limits about 11 times the SM rate as of 2025.

topic_review.cite: ATLAS Collaboration, Characterising the Higgs boson with ATLAS data from Run 2 of the LHC, Physics Reports, 2025

problems.title: Does the top-Higgs coupling contain a CP-violating component?
problems.plain: The SM predicts that the interaction between the Higgs and the top quark respects CP, the combined mirror and particle-antiparticle symmetry. A CP-violating part would be a new source of the matter-antimatter difference.
problems.precise: With L ~ -(y_t/sqrt 2) kappa_t h tbar (cos alpha + i gamma_5 sin alpha) t, the SM has $\alpha = 0$. ATLAS ttH and tH with $H \to \gamma \gamma$ excludes $\mid\alpha\mid > 43\ \mathrm{deg}$ at 95 percent CL (Phys. Rev. Lett. 125, 061802, 2020). An answer is alpha determined to a few degrees, or a bound which, combined with electron EDM limits, decides whether top-Higgs CP violation can supply electroweak baryogenesis.
problems.settled_by: HL-LHC angular analyses of ttH and tH production in several Higgs decay channels, combined with EDM limits on the loop-induced CP-odd operators.
problems.status_note: LHC Run 2 data agree with $\alpha = 0$ and exclude a purely CP-odd top Yukawa coupling.

links.reason: Electron EDM bounds constrain CP-violating top-Higgs couplings through two-loop Barr-Zee diagrams.

problems.title: Is the Higgs total decay width equal to the SM 4.1 MeV?
problems.plain: The width of the Higgs measures how fast it decays and counts every decay, including decays to unknown particles. The SM predicts 4.1 MeV, far too narrow to resolve directly at the LHC.
problems.precise: Determine $\Gamma_H$ with $\le 5\%$ uncertainty (SM: $4.1\ \mathrm{MeV}$). CMS used off-shell $H* \to \mathrm{ZZ}$ production to obtain $\Gamma_H=3.2+2.4-1.7\ \mathrm{MeV}$ (Nature Physics 18, 1329, 2022), a method that assumes equal coupling modifiers on and off shell. An answer is a model-independent $\Gamma_H$, which bounds the total rate of undetected and invisible decays.
problems.settled_by: A Higgs-factory measurement of $\sigma(e+ e- \to \mathrm{ZH})$ by the recoil-mass method combined with $\mathrm{BR}(H \to \mathrm{ZZ}*)$ or $\mathrm{BR}(H \to \mathrm{WW}*)$, giving $\Gamma_H$ without model assumptions at the percent level.
problems.status_note: The 2022 CMS off-shell result agrees with the SM within errors of about 60 percent.

topic_review.cite: ATLAS Collaboration, Characterising the Higgs boson with ATLAS data from Run 2 of the LHC, Physics Reports, 2025

problems.title: Was the electroweak phase transition first order?
problems.plain: In the SM, the Higgs field switched on smoothly as the early universe cooled. New particles could instead have made it an abrupt boiling transition, which could produce the matter excess and gravitational waves.
problems.precise: Lattice results show the SM electroweak transition is a crossover for $m_h = 125\,\mathrm{GeV}$. Determine whether nature has BSM scalars or couplings that make it strongly first order, $v(T_c)/T_c > \sim 1$. An answer identifies the order of the transition from measured Higgs potential parameters or excludes all first-order scenarios with a singlet or doublet extension.
problems.settled_by: A measurement of $\kappa_{\lambda}$ and of Higgs-singlet mixing at future colliders, or detection of a stochastic gravitational-wave background peaked near mHz by LISA.

problems.title: How precisely does the measured top mass equal the pole mass?
problems.plain: Colliders extract the top-quark mass by matching data to computer event simulations, and that parameter is not exactly the mass defined in theory calculations. The mismatch is now as large as the measurement errors.
problems.precise: Quantify the relation $m_t^{\mathrm{MC}} = m_t^{\mathrm{pole}} + \Delta$ between the top mass parameter of parton-shower event generators and the pole (or MSR) mass, including the $\operatorname{O}(\Lambda_{\mathrm{QCD}})$ renormalon ambiguity of the pole mass. An answer is Delta with uncertainty below $\sim 0.3\,\mathrm{GeV}$ and a calibration usable by LHC analyses.
problems.settled_by: First-principles calculations of parton-shower mass schemes calibrated against hadron-level NNLL plus NNLO predictions of top-mass-sensitive observables.
problems.status_note: Calibration studies (2018 to 2025) estimate $\Delta$ of order $0.5\,\mathrm{GeV}$ with comparable uncertainty.

problems.title: What is the Higgs trilinear self-coupling?
problems.plain: The Higgs interacts with itself, and the SM predicts the exact strength from the Higgs mass. Measuring it requires seeing Higgs bosons produced in pairs, an extremely rare process.
problems.precise: Measure $\kappa_{\lambda} = \lambda_3/\lambda_3^{\mathrm{SM}}$, where the SM gives $\lambda_3 = m_h^2/(2 v^2) \sim 0.13$ for the cubic term $\lambda_3 v h^3$. An answer is $\kappa_{\lambda}$ with total uncertainty below about 0.3 (30 percent), sufficient to distinguish the SM from models with a strongly first-order phase transition.
problems.settled_by: Combined HH production at the HL-LHC (projected about 30 to 50 percent precision) and at a future collider (FCC-hh projected $\sim 5$ percent).
problems.status_note: The 2026 ATLAS plus CMS Run 2 HH combination (arXiv:2602.23991) gives $-0.71 < \kappa_{\lambda} < 6.1$ at 95 percent CL (expected -1.3 to 6.7) and HH signal strength $0.8 +0.9/-0.7$, an observed significance of $1.1\sigma$.

problems.title: Is the electroweak vacuum absolutely stable if the SM holds to $M_{\mathrm{Pl}}$?
problems.plain: If no new particles appear up to the Planck scale, the measured Higgs and top-quark masses seem to make our vacuum only long-lived instead of permanently stable. The verdict depends on the top mass to a fraction of a GeV.
problems.precise: In the SM with three-loop RG running and two-loop matching, determine whether the effective Higgs quartic stays positive for all field values up to and beyond $M_{\mathrm{Pl}}$. Absolute stability requires a top pole mass near $171.1\,\mathrm{GeV}$, about $1.5\,\mathrm{GeV}$ below the direct-measurement average $172.57 \pm 0.29\,\mathrm{GeV}$, or $\alpha_s(m_Z)$ near 0.1213 instead of 0.1180 (Hiller et al. 2024); the answer is the classification stable, metastable or unstable at $5\sigma$.
problems.settled_by: A top-quark pole mass determination with uncertainty $\sim 0.1\,\mathrm{GeV}$ (for example from a $t-\mathrm{tbar}$ threshold scan at an $e+e-$ collider) together with $\alpha_{s}(m_{Z})$ to $\sim 0.1\%$.
problems.status_note: Hiller, Hohne, Litim and Steudtner (arXiv:2401.08811, revised 2026) find stability disfavored by $1.9\,\sigma$ with the cross-section pole mass $172.4 \pm 0.7\,\mathrm{GeV}$ and by $5.1\,\sigma$ if the template-fit mass $172.57 \pm 0.29\,\mathrm{GeV}$ is taken as the pole mass; reducing the $m_{t}$ and $\alpha_{s}$ errors by a factor of 2 to 3 would settle it at $5\,\sigma$.

problems.title: What microscopic process produces the excess in cryogenic calorimeters?
problems.plain: Crystals cooled near absolute zero record many more small heat pulses below a few hundred electron volts than expected, and the rate fades over weeks after cooling. The question is what inside the detector releases this energy.
problems.precise: Cryogenic calorimeters (CRESST $\mathrm{CaWO_4}$, $\mathrm{Al_2O_3}$, Si; SuperCDMS-type Si and Ge; NUCLEUS; EDELWEISS) observe a rate $\mathrm{d}R/\mathrm{d}E$ rising steeply below about 200 eV, uncorrelated with particle backgrounds and decaying after cooldown. Candidate sources include stress relaxation at holders, glue and sensor films; dislocation motion from differential thermal contraction; and annealing of radiation-induced lattice defects. An answer is a mechanism that reproduces the energy spectrum, the time dependence, the material dependence and the sensor-geometry dependence, confirmed by a controlled test that turns the excess on or off.
problems.settled_by: A detector in which removing or adding the hypothesized source (e.g., stress in the holder or film, or a defect population) changes the excess rate by a predicted factor.
problems.status_note: In 2026 NUCLEUS (Eur. Phys. J. C 86, 831) found slower cooldown lowers the initial rate and the rate decays as a power law independent of particle background; stress-relaxation (Nature Commun. 2024), thermal-contraction (2026 preprint) and defect-annealing (Phys. Rev. Mater. 2025) explanations all remain under discussion.

Non-radiative phonon bursts would add correlated qubit errors beyond ionizing radiation.
Stress relaxation and phonon bursts may produce both calorimeter excess and excess quasiparticles.

problems.title: What sets the residual single-electron event rate in skipper CCDs?
problems.plain: Skipper CCDs can count single electrons, but they register stray single electrons at a low steady rate that mimics the faintest dark matter signals. The question is where these stray electrons come from and how low the rate can go.
problems.precise: Skipper CCDs (SENSEI, DAMIC-M, Oscura) measure a rate of 1-electron events per pixel per day that limits searches for dark matter-electron scattering in the 1-2 electron bins. Candidate sources are thermal dark current, spurious charge from readout clocking, Cherenkov and recombination photons from high-energy tracks, and charge release from defects. An answer is a quantitative decomposition of the measured rate into sources and the irreducible floor for silicon at the operating temperature.
problems.settled_by: Rate measurements versus temperature, clocking scheme, readout timing, shielding and track density in otherwise identical CCDs, compared with a calibrated source model.
problems.status_note: The 2025 DAMIC-M prototype search (Phys. Rev. Lett. 135, 071002) ran with a 50-fold lower single-electron rate than its previous search, showing much of the earlier rate was instrumental; the floor is not known.

topic_review.cite: P. Adari, A. A. Aguilar-Arevalo, D. Amidei, G. Angloher et al., EXCESS workshop: Descriptions of rising low-energy spectra, SciPost Phys. Proc. 9, 001, 2022

problems.title: What causes the bulk ionization excess in DAMIC CCDs at SNOLAB?
problems.plain: Silicon camera chips used to search for dark matter deep underground see extra small charge signals from inside the silicon, beyond all known radioactivity. The cause is unknown.
problems.precise: DAMIC at SNOLAB reported an excess of bulk ionization events above the radiogenic background model, with characteristic rate about 7 events/(kg day) at electron-equivalent energies about 80 eV, later confirmed with skipper CCDs. An answer identifies the source (unmodeled background such as low-energy Compton or surface events, a detector effect, or new physics) and predicts the rate and spectrum in other silicon detectors.
problems.settled_by: Comparison of the bulk excess across silicon CCDs with different fabrication, depth, shielding and cosmogenic exposure (DAMIC-M, SENSEI, Oscura prototypes) and with calibrated low-energy Compton spectra.
problems.status_note: Confirmed with skipper CCDs at SNOLAB (Phys. Rev. D 109, 062007, 2024, arXiv 2306.01717); origin unknown.

topic_review.cite: P. Adari, A. A. Aguilar-Arevalo, D. Amidei, G. Angloher et al., EXCESS workshop: Descriptions of rising low-energy spectra, SciPost Phys. Proc. 9, 001, 2022

problems.title: Do single-sensor and shared excess events have different origins?
problems.plain: When two sensors are mounted on the same crystal, some excess events show up in only one sensor and others in both. Deciding whether these come from the sensor or from the crystal narrows the cause.
problems.precise: In two-channel athermal phonon detectors, excess events split into 'singles' (energy in one sensor only) and 'shared' events (energy in both, absorber-like). The question is whether singles originate in the sensor films (e.g., stress in the superconducting film, quasiparticle bursts) and shared events in the absorber or its mounting, and what fraction of each survives in a stress-free, glue-free mount.
problems.settled_by: Multi-sensor detectors with varied film thickness, film material and mounting, measuring the singles and shared rates and their time dependence separately.
problems.status_note: Anthony-Petersen et al. (Nature Commun. 2024) linked a large part of the shared-event excess in a two-channel Si detector to holder-induced stress; the source of singles and of the remaining shared events is not settled.

topic_review.cite: P. Adari, A. A. Aguilar-Arevalo, D. Amidei, G. Angloher et al., EXCESS workshop: Descriptions of rising low-energy spectra, SciPost Phys. Proc. 9, 001, 2022

problems.title: What law governs the decay and reset of the excess rate?
problems.plain: The excess fades in the weeks and months after a detector is cooled and partly returns if it is warmed and cooled again. The precise shape of this fading is a clue to its cause.
problems.precise: Let $R(t)$ be the excess event rate above threshold at time $t$ after the end of cooldown. Data from CRESST-III and NUCLEUS have been described by sums of exponentials with time constants of tens to hundreds of days and by power laws $R \sim t^{-\alpha}$. The question is the functional form of $R(t)$, its dependence on cooldown rate and on the maximum temperature of an intermediate warm-up, and whether these match a relaxation model (e.g., a distribution of activation barriers in a glassy stress or defect system).
problems.settled_by: Long continuous runs on identical detectors with controlled cooldown rates and warm-up temperatures, fitted against competing relaxation models.
problems.status_note: NUCLEUS (Eur. Phys. J. C 86, 831, 2026) found $R(t)$ best described by a power law with common exponent $-0.59 \pm 0.06$, with $t$ measured from reaching 4 K, and lower initial rates after slower cooldown.

problems.title: Does the measured solar 8B CEvNS rate in xenon match the Standard Model?
problems.plain: Xenon dark matter detectors have begun to see solar neutrinos gently bumping whole xenon nuclei, a process called coherent scattering. The question is whether the measured rate equals the Standard Model prediction or hints at new neutrino interactions.
problems.precise: Coherent elastic neutrino-nucleus scattering (CEvNS) of solar 8B neutrinos on Xe produces nuclear recoils below a few keV. The quantity is the measured 8B flux (or CEvNS rate) inferred from xenon data, compared with the SM cross section and the solar-model and SNO flux of about $5.2 \times 10^{6}\ \mathrm{cm}^{-2}\ \mathrm{s}^{-1}$. An answer is a measurement with 10 percent precision and the resulting bound on nonstandard neutrino-quark couplings or light mediators.
problems.settled_by: A xenon (or argon) detector measurement of the 8B CEvNS rate with low enough threshold and calibrated nuclear-recoil response to reach about 10 percent uncertainty.
problems.status_note: XENONnT ($2.73\sigma$) and PandaX-4T ($2.64\sigma$) reported evidence in 2024 (Phys. Rev. Lett. 133, 191002 and 191001); in 2026 LZ reported $4.5\sigma$ (Phys. Rev. Lett. 137, 091806) and XENONnT $3.3\sigma$ with flux $(5 +3 -2)e6\ \mathrm{cm}^{-2}\ \mathrm{s}^{-1}$ (Phys. Rev. Lett. 137, 091807); flux uncertainties remain about 50 percent.

problems.title: How well is the sub-100 MeV atmospheric neutrino flux known?
problems.plain: For heavy dark matter, the main neutrino background comes from cosmic rays hitting the atmosphere and producing low-energy neutrinos, whose number is poorly measured. Better knowledge of this flux decides how deep heavy dark matter searches can go.
problems.precise:
The CEvNS background for WIMP masses above about $100\,\mathrm{GeV}$ comes from atmospheric neutrinos with $E_
u$ below about $100\,\mathrm{MeV}$, where the flux has never been measured directly and model uncertainties are of order 20 percent. The quantity is this flux, with its site and solar-cycle dependence, to about 10 percent precision. An answer is a measurement or a validated calculation of the sub-$100\,\mathrm{MeV}$ atmospheric $
u_e$ and $
u_\mu$ fluxes at underground laboratory sites.
problems.settled_by: A measurement of low-energy atmospheric neutrinos in a large detector (e.g., JUNO, Super-Kamiokande with gadolinium, DUNE) or by the first atmospheric CEvNS detection in a dark matter detector.
problems.status_note: Fan, Liu and Zhou (Chin. Phys. C 49, 103001, 2025) estimated the atmospheric flux at CJPL to be about 30 percent lower than at LNGS, so the fog boundary for heavy WIMPs is site dependent.

problems.title: Can recoil direction separate dark matter from solar neutrinos?
problems.plain: Solar neutrinos push nuclei away from the Sun, while dark matter pushes them along Earth's path through the galaxy. A detector that measures recoil directions could tell them apart, if it can track recoils only a few keV in energy.
problems.precise: In the neutrino fog, defined by O'Hare as the region where the discovery-limit index $n = -(d \ln \sigma / d \ln \mathrm{exposure})^{-1}$ exceeds 2, sensitivity grows slower than $1/\sqrt{\mathrm{exposure}}$. The question is the angular resolution, head-tail recognition efficiency and threshold (e.g., in a He:$\mathrm{SF_6}$ or $\mathrm{CF_4}$ gas time projection chamber) needed to restore n near 1 at WIMP masses 5-10 GeV and cross sections about one order of magnitude below the 8B fog boundary for the chosen target, and the exposure this requires.
problems.settled_by: Demonstrated head-tail sensitivity and angular resolution for few-keV nuclear recoils in a prototype, combined with a sensitivity calculation using the measured performance.

topic_review.cite: C. A. J. O'Hare, New Definition of the Neutrino Floor for Direct Dark Matter Searches, Phys. Rev. Lett. 127, 251802, 2021

problems.title: Can direct detection reach thermal higgsino dark matter above the fog?
problems.plain: A leading heavy dark matter candidate, the higgsino from supersymmetry, would weigh about 1.1 TeV and interact very weakly with nuclei. The question is whether its scattering rate lies above the neutrino background where detectors can still find it.
problems.precise: For a nearly pure higgsino with thermal relic mass near 1.1 TeV, the spin-independent cross section $\sigma_{SI}$ comes from loop diagrams and from tree-level mixing suppressed by the bino and wino masses $M_1$, $M_2$. The question is $\sigma_{SI}$ as a function of $M_1$, $M_2$ and $\tan\beta$, including higher-order QCD and nuclear matrix-element uncertainties, compared with the xenon and argon neutrino-fog boundary at 1.1 TeV. An answer states for which gaugino masses a planned xenon or argon detector of about 1000 tonne-year exposure has $3\sigma$ discovery reach.
problems.settled_by: Extension of the heavy-WIMP effective theory NLO computation (Hill and Solon, Phys. Rev. D 91, 043505, 2015) to gaugino-mixed higgsinos, mapping $\sigma_{\mathrm{SI}}(M_1, M_2, \tan \beta)$ with hadronic uncertainties against the xenon and argon fog boundary at $1.1\,\mathrm{TeV}$.
problems.status_note: The pure-higgsino limit was computed at NLO by Hill and Solon (2015); the mixing-dependent reach is not mapped against the fog.

problems.title: What is the mass of the lightest neutrino?
problems.plain: Oscillations measure only differences of neutrino masses. The overall scale must come from precise $\beta$ decay spectra or from how neutrinos affected the growth of cosmic structure.
problems.precise: Determine $m_{\mathrm{lightest}}$, or equivalently $m_{\beta}=(\sum\left|U_{ei}\right|^{2}m_i^{2})^{1/2}$ and $\sum m_{\nu}$. KATRIN (2025) gives $m_{\beta}<0.45\ \mathrm{eV}$ (90 percent CL); oscillations require $\sum m_{\nu}\ge \sim 0.059\ \mathrm{eV}$ (normal) or $\sim 0.10\ \mathrm{eV}$ (inverted). An answer is a nonzero value with $\sim 20\%$ uncertainty or a consistent upper limit across laboratory and cosmology.
problems.settled_by: Cosmological detection of sum $m_{\nu}$ at $\ge 3\sigma$ (DESI, Euclid, CMB-S4) cross-checked by a laboratory direct measurement (Project 8 or successors) reaching $m_{\beta} \sim 40\,\mathrm{meV}$.
problems.status_note: DESI DR2 plus CMB (2025) gives sum $m_{\nu} < 0.064\,\mathrm{eV}$ (95 percent, LCDM), in tension with the oscillation minimum; the tension relaxes in evolving dark energy fits.

problems.title: Are neutrinos Majorana particles, their own antiparticles?
problems.plain: If a neutrino is its own antiparticle, certain nuclei could undergo a double beta decay that emits no neutrinos at all. Its observation would show that lepton number is not conserved.
problems.precise: Determine whether lepton number is violated by Majorana neutrino masses via neutrinoless double beta decay, with half-life T_1/2 $\sim 10^{26}$ to $10^{28}$ yr for $m_{bb} \sim 10\ \text{to}\ 50\ \mathrm{meV}$. KamLAND-Zen (2024) gives T_1/2(Xe-136) > $3.8 \times 10^{26}$ yr, $m_{bb} < \sim 28\ \text{to}\ 122\ \mathrm{meV}$ (spread from nuclear matrix elements).
problems.settled_by: Ton-scale double beta decay experiments (LEGEND-1000, nEXO, CUPID, KamLAND2-Zen) covering the inverted-ordering band $m_{bb} \sim 15\text{ to }50\,\mathrm{meV}$.

problems.title: Is the neutrino mass ordering normal or inverted?
problems.plain: We know the mass differences between the three neutrinos but not whether the odd one out is heaviest (normal ordering) or lightest (inverted ordering).
problems.precise: Determine the sign of $\Delta m^2_{31}$ ($\left|\Delta m^2_{31}\right| \sim 2.5 \times 10^{-3}\,\mathrm{eV}^2$) at $\ge 3\,\sigma$ from reactor oscillation spectra (JUNO), matter effects in long-baseline accelerator (DUNE, Hyper-K) and atmospheric data. Answer: normal or inverted.
problems.settled_by: JUNO reactor spectral data over about 6 years combined with DUNE and atmospheric experiments.
problems.status_note: JUNO 207-day data combined with long-baseline accelerator $\Delta m^{2}_{31}$ constraints (arXiv:2609.37895, September 2026) favor normal ordering at one-sided $\ge 2.1\sigma$ for all $\delta_{\mathrm{CP}}$ (Bayes factor 10.18); global fits (NuFit-6.0, 2024) also lean normal; the 2025 NOvA plus T2K joint fit prefers neither.

problems.title: What mechanism generates neutrino masses?
problems.plain: Neutrinos are at least a million times lighter than the electron. They could get mass like other particles but with a tiny coupling, or through a seesaw with very heavy partner particles.
problems.precise: Identify the origin of $m_{\nu} < \sim 0.1\ \mathrm{eV}$: Dirac Yukawas with $y \sim 10^{-12}$ plus right-handed neutrinos, the type I, II or III seesaw ($m_{\nu} \sim y^2 v^2 / M$), or radiative and low-scale mechanisms. An answer is the mechanism together with its scale, confirmed by a signature such as lepton number violation or heavy neutral leptons.
problems.settled_by: Observation of neutrinoless double beta decay plus identification of the associated new states or interactions at colliders or in rare decays.

topic_review.cite: I. Esteban, M. C. Gonzalez-Garcia, M. Maltoni, I. Martinez-Soler, J. P. Pinheiro, T. Schwetz, NuFit-6.0: updated global analysis of three-flavor neutrino oscillations, JHEP, 2024

problems.title: Is $\theta_{23}$ maximal, and if not, in which octant?
problems.plain: Muon-type and tau-type neutrinos are mixed in nearly equal amounts, but it is unknown whether the mixing angle is exactly 45 degrees or slightly above or below it. Exactly 45 degrees would point to a hidden symmetry between muons and taus.
problems.precise: Determine $\sin^{2}(\theta_{23})$ in the three-flavor PMNS framework to about $\pm 0.01$ and decide at $\ge 3\sigma$ whether $\theta_{23}=45\ \mathrm{deg}$ is excluded and, if so, whether $\theta_{23}<45\ \mathrm{deg}$ (lower octant) or $>45\ \mathrm{deg}$ (upper octant). NuFit-6.0 finds local minima near $\sin^{2}(\theta_{23})\sim 0.47$ and $\sim 0.56$ separated by $\Delta \chi^{2}<4$ for both mass orderings and both data variants (approximate).
problems.settled_by: DUNE and Hyper-Kamiokande $\nu_{\mu}$ disappearance and $\nu_{e}$ appearance data, using the reactor value of $\theta_{13}$, combined with atmospheric data from IceCube and KM3NeT/ORCA.
problems.status_note: NuFit-6.0 (2024) leaves the octant unresolved, with the other-octant minimum always within $\Delta \chi^{2} < 4$.

problems.title: What causes the short-baseline neutrino anomalies?
problems.plain: LSND and MiniBooNE saw extra electron-like events, and gallium detectors saw too few neutrino captures. These do not fit the three-neutrino picture.
problems.precise: Explain the LSND (1995) and MiniBooNE electron-like excesses and the gallium deficit in a single consistent framework, or show they have separate conventional origins. An answer is the mechanism (sterile oscillation, decaying heavy states, new interactions, or background and cross-section mismodeling) consistent with disappearance limits.
problems.settled_by: The Fermilab SBN program (SBND, MicroBooNE, ICARUS) measuring $\nu_e$ appearance and $\nu_\mu$ disappearance with one technology at several baselines.
problems.status_note: MicroBooNE (Nature, December 2025) excludes a single light sterile neutrino explanation of LSND and MiniBooNE at 95 percent CL.

problems.title: Does an eV-scale sterile neutrino exist?
problems.plain: A fourth neutrino that feels no force except gravity, with mass near 1 eV, could explain some anomalies. It would show up as extra appearance and disappearance at short distances.
problems.precise: Determine whether a fourth mass state with $\Delta m^2_{41} \sim 0.1 \text{ to } 10\,\mathrm{eV}^2$ and mixings |U_e4|, |U_mu4| large enough to produce sin^2(2 theta_mue) $\sim 10^{-3}$ exists. An answer is a $5\,\sigma$ oscillation signal or exclusion of the region preferred by LSND and gallium in both appearance and disappearance.
problems.settled_by: Combined SBN-program oscillation fits with near and far detectors, plus reactor (PROSPECT, STEREO) and atmospheric (IceCube) disappearance limits.
problems.status_note: Appearance-disappearance tension in global fits and the 2025 MicroBooNE result disfavor the simple 3+1 model.

problems.title: Why do gallium detectors see about 20 percent fewer neutrino captures?
problems.plain: Experiments placing strong radioactive neutrino sources inside gallium consistently record fewer captures than predicted. The cause, new physics or a wrong cross section, is unknown.
problems.precise: The BEST (2022), GALLEX and SAGE source experiments measure $R = \mathrm{observed}/\mathrm{predicted} \sim 0.8$ for Ga-71(nu_e, e-)Ge-71 with Cr-51 and Ar-37 sources, about $4\sigma$ below 1. Determine whether the deficit comes from the capture cross section (Ge-71 excited-state transitions, half-life), the source activity, or oscillation, in tension with reactor and solar limits.
problems.settled_by: An independent source experiment with a different target and an improved measurement of the Ga-71 to Ge-71 matrix elements and Ge-71 half-life.
problems.status_note: Remeasurements of the Ge-71 half-life (2023 to 2024) did not remove the deficit; sterile oscillation explanations conflict with reactor and solar data.

problems.title: What is the source of the MiniBooNE low-energy excess?
problems.plain: MiniBooNE saw extra events at low energy that look like electrons, but its detector could not tell electrons from photons.
problems.precise: Identify whether the MiniBooNE low-energy excess (reconstructed $E_{\nu}$ between 200 and 475 MeV) is from electrons, single photons, e+e- pairs or mismodeled backgrounds such as $\Delta \to \mathrm{N}\gamma$ and $\pi0$ misidentification. An answer assigns the excess to a specific final state with $\ge 3\sigma$ confidence.
problems.settled_by: Liquid-argon TPC measurements in the same beam that separate electrons from photons by dE/dx (MicroBooNE, SBND, ICARUS).
problems.status_note: MicroBooNE results (2021 to 2025) disfavor $\nu_e$ and $\Delta$ radiative explanations of the full excess, leaving its source unidentified.

problems.title: How is the Peccei-Quinn symmetry protected from gravitational breaking?
problems.plain: The axion solution needs a symmetry to be almost exact, but gravity is expected to break all such global symmetries slightly. Even a tiny breaking would spoil the solution.
problems.precise: Planck-suppressed operators $O \sim \Phi^n / M_{\mathrm{Pl}}^{(n-4)}$ shift $\theta_{\mathrm{bar}}$ by $\sim f_a^n / (M_{\mathrm{Pl}}^{(n-4)} m_a^2 f_a^2)$; keeping $\mid\theta_{\mathrm{bar}}\mid < 10^{-10}$ for $f_a \sim 10^{10}\,\mathrm{GeV}$ requires $n > \sim 10$. An answer is a UV mechanism (gauge discrete symmetries, composite or extra-dimensional axions) that provably forbids operators up to the required n with predicted low-energy signatures.
problems.settled_by: A UV-complete model with the required protection and a distinct prediction, for example heavy axions or modified axion couplings, confirmed by experiment.

problems.title: Does the QCD axion exist?
problems.plain: The axion would be a very light, very weakly interacting particle that removes the strong CP puzzle. Detectors search for it turning into a photon inside strong magnets.
problems.precise: Determine whether a pseudoscalar a with $m_a \sim 5.7\ \mathrm{micro-eV}\ (10^{12}\ \mathrm{GeV}/f_a)$ and photon coupling $g_{agamma}$ inside the QCD axion band (KSVZ to DFSZ and beyond) exists, for $f_a\ \text{between}\ \sim 10^{8}\ \text{and}\ \sim 10^{17}\ \mathrm{GeV}$. An answer is a detection with $m_a$ and $g_{agamma}$ consistent with the QCD mass-decay constant relation, or exclusion of the band over the full range.
problems.settled_by: Haloscope, helioscope (IAXO) and nuclear-coupling (CASPEr-type) searches covering the QCD axion band across micro-eV to meV masses.
problems.status_note: Haloscopes reach DFSZ sensitivity only in narrow windows of a few micro-eV as of 2025.

topic_review.cite: L. Di Luzio, M. Giannotti, E. Nardi, L. Visinelli, The landscape of QCD axion models, Physics Reports, 2020

problems.title: Does a nonzero $\theta$ produce observable CP violation in QCD?
problems.plain: A few theorists argue that, done carefully, the strong-force theory never produces the forbidden effects, so there is no puzzle. Most others say the standard reasoning holds, and the disagreement has not been settled.
problems.precise: Determine whether CP-odd observables in QCD ($d_{n}$, the $\theta$ dependence of the vacuum energy and of hadron matrix elements) depend on $\theta_{\mathrm{bar}}$ when the infinite-volume limit and the sum over topological sectors are taken in the order argued by Ai, Cruz, Garbrecht and Tamarit (arXiv:2001.07152). An answer is a proof or a lattice computation showing $d_{n}$ proportional to $\theta_{\mathrm{bar}}$, or the opposite.
problems.settled_by: A rigorous treatment of the $\theta$-dependence of CP-odd correlators in QCD, cross-checked by lattice computations of $d_n$ at imaginary or small real $\theta$.
problems.status_note: Benabou, Hook, Manzari, Murayama and Safdi (arXiv:2510.18951, 2025) and Khoze (arXiv:2512.06827, 2025) argue $\theta$ is physical; Ai, Garbrecht and Tamarit replied (arXiv:2511.04216, 2025) and the exchange continues in 2026 (arXiv:2601.18248); the majority view keeps the strong CP problem.

problems.title: Why is the QCD $\theta$ angle smaller than $10^{-10}$?
problems.plain: The strong-force angle $\theta$ could have any value up to about 3, yet the neutron's electric dipole moment shows it is below $10^{-10}$. No reason for this is known.
problems.precise: The physical parameter $\theta_{\mathrm{bar}} = \theta - \arg \det(M_{q})$ induces $d_{n} \sim 10^{-16}\ \theta_{\mathrm{bar}}\ e\ \mathrm{cm}$; the PSI bound $\mid d_{n}\mid < 1.8 \times 10^{-26}\ e\ \mathrm{cm}$ (90 percent CL, 2020) gives $\mid\theta_{\mathrm{bar}}\mid < \sim 10^{-10}$. An answer is a mechanism (Peccei-Quinn axion, massless up quark, spontaneous CP or P violation such as Nelson-Barr) consistent with lattice QCD and flavor data.
problems.settled_by: Detection of the QCD axion with the predicted mass-coupling relation, or a confirmed alternative such as a nonzero measured $d_n$ with the pattern predicted by a Nelson-Barr model.
problems.status_note: Lattice QCD (2010s to 2020s) excludes $m_{u} = 0$, removing the massless up quark solution.

problems.title: Can daily modulation in anisotropic crystals identify light dark matter?
problems.plain: In a crystal that responds differently along different directions, the signal from dark matter should rise and fall once a day as Earth rotates, while most backgrounds should not. This could distinguish a real signal from the unexplained excess of small events.
problems.precise: For sub-GeV dark matter scattering via phonons or electrons in anisotropic crystals (e.g., $\mathrm{Al_2O_3}$, hexagonal BN, graphene-like or Dirac materials), the rate $R(t)$ modulates with sidereal period because the dark matter wind direction rotates relative to the crystal axes; predicted fractional amplitudes reach tens of percent in some materials. The question is whether a modulation of this size can be measured at sub-eV thresholds with exposure below about $1\,\mathrm{kg}\,\mathrm{yr}$, given present low-energy excess rates, and whether the excess itself shows any sidereal modulation.
problems.settled_by: A sidereal-period analysis of a low-threshold anisotropic-crystal data set with known orientation, giving an amplitude limit or detection at the predicted level.
problems.status_note: A 2026 preprint (arXiv 2606.04091) estimated halo-model uncertainties of 1-100 percent in single-phonon rates across the mass range, which enter the modulation prediction.

topic_review.cite: Y. Kahn and T. Lin, Searches for light dark matter using condensed matter systems, Rep. Prog. Phys. 85, 066901, 2022

problems.title: Can detectors reach the sub-MeV freeze-in dark matter benchmark?
problems.plain: In one favored scenario, light dark matter was slowly produced in the early universe through a very light force carrier, which fixes how often it should scatter off electrons. Silicon detectors now exclude this scenario over much of the MeV to GeV range, but lighter dark matter carries too little energy to free an electron in silicon.
problems.precise: In the freeze-in benchmark with an ultralight dark-photon mediator, the DM-electron cross section $\sigma_e(m_{\chi})$ is fixed by the relic abundance. For $m_{\chi}$ below about 1 MeV the kinetic energy $(1/2) m_{\chi} v^2$ with $v \sim 10^{-3} c$ is below the 1.1 eV silicon gap, so semiconductor targets lose sensitivity. The question is whether a target with meV-scale gap or collective response (superconductors, Dirac materials, polar crystals via in-medium dark-photon mixing, superconducting nanowires) reaches the freeze-in line for $m_{\chi} = 10\,\mathrm{keV} - 1\,\mathrm{MeV}$, accounting for in-medium screening.
problems.settled_by: An exposure-scaled limit from a low-gap target that crosses the freeze-in line, with in-medium dielectric response measured or computed for that material.
problems.status_note: DAMIC-M (Phys. Rev. Lett. 135, 071002, 2025) excluded freeze-in and freeze-out benchmarks over large ranges below 1 GeV; QROCODILE (Phys. Rev. Lett. 2025) set first sub-MeV limits with a 0.11 eV threshold, still far from the sub-MeV freeze-in line.

topic_review.cite: Y. Kahn and T. Lin, Searches for light dark matter using condensed matter systems, Rep. Prog. Phys. 85, 066901, 2022

problems.title: Can single-magnon counting probe spin-coupled sub-MeV dark matter?
problems.plain: In a magnet, spins can ripple together as a wave whose smallest unit is a magnon; dark matter that couples to electron spins could create one. Single magnons have been detected with a quantum bit, but no detector yet has the size and low noise needed for a dark matter search.
problems.precise: Dark matter of mass $m_{\chi} \sim 1\,\mathrm{keV} - 1\,\mathrm{MeV}$ coupling to electron spin (e.g., via an axial-vector or magnetic-dipole interaction) excites gapped magnons of energy 1-100 meV in ordered magnets such as YIG, with rates computed by Trickle, Zhang and Zurek (Phys. Rev. Lett. 124, 201801, 2020). Single-magnon detection by a superconducting qubit was demonstrated with quantum efficiency up to 0.71 in a mm-scale ferrimagnetic crystal (Lachance-Quirion et al. 2020). The question is whether magnon counting can be scaled to target mass of about 1 kg with dark-count rate low enough to cross existing astrophysical bounds on spin-dependent couplings.
problems.settled_by: A gram-scale or larger magnon detector with measured single-magnon dark-count rate, followed by a published dark matter limit.

topic_review.cite: Y. Kahn and T. Lin, Searches for light dark matter using condensed matter systems, Rep. Prog. Phys. 85, 066901, 2022

problems.title: Does the Migdal effect occur at the predicted rate in detector media?
problems.plain: When a nucleus is hit suddenly, its electrons may be shaken loose, giving a detectable signal even from very light dark matter; this is the Migdal effect. It has now been seen directly, but searches in liquid xenon have not found it at the predicted rate.
problems.precise: The Migdal effect is ionization or excitation of atomic electrons following an abrupt nuclear recoil, with probability predicted by Ibe et al. (2018) for isolated atoms and by solid-state calculations for crystals. The quantity is the ratio of the Migdal ionization cross section to the elastic nuclear-recoil cross section, measured with neutron beams, in liquid xenon, liquid argon and silicon or germanium crystals, compared with theory. An answer is this ratio to about 20 percent in each medium.
problems.settled_by: Neutron-scattering measurements with tagged nuclear recoils in each target medium, extracting the Migdal rate per recoil and its electron-energy spectrum.
problems.status_note: Yi et al. (Nature 649, 580, 2026) reported a $5\sigma$ observation in neutron scattering (6 candidate events) with Migdal to nuclear-recoil cross-section ratio $4.9 (+2.6 -1.9)e-5$; a liquid xenon search (Xu et al., Phys. Rev. D 109, L051101, 2024) saw no signal at the predicted level, and an LZ thesis analysis quotes a 90 percent limit at 26 percent of the Ibe et al. prediction.

topic_review.cite: Y. Kahn and T. Lin, Searches for light dark matter using condensed matter systems, Rep. Prog. Phys. 85, 066901, 2022

problems.title: Can calorimeters detect single optical phonons with low background?
problems.plain: Dark matter between about a hundred and a hundred thousand times lighter than a proton would make a crystal vibrate with only one quantum of vibration energy, a few hundredths of an electron volt. Detectors are not yet sensitive enough to count these single quanta.
problems.precise: Dark matter of mass $m_{\chi} \sim 10\,\mathrm{keV} - 10\,\mathrm{MeV}$ scattering via a dark-photon or hadrophilic mediator excites single optical or acoustic phonons of energy $\omega \sim 10-100\,\mathrm{meV}$ in polar crystals (GaAs, $\mathrm{Al_2O_3}$, $\mathrm{SiO_2}$). The question is whether a phonon sensor (transition-edge sensor, kinetic-inductance detector, superconducting qubit) can reach an energy threshold below 100 meV with dark-count rate below about 1 event/(kg day) at that threshold. An answer is a demonstrated threshold and background, or a proof-of-limit from sensor noise and phonon down-conversion losses.
problems.settled_by: A calibrated single-phonon-scale threshold measured in a gram-scale crystal underground, with the background rate measured at that threshold.
problems.status_note: TESSERACT (Phys. Rev. Lett. 2025) set first limits for 44-87 MeV dark matter with an athermal phonon detector at eV-scale threshold; single-phonon sensitivity is not demonstrated, and the low-energy excess sets the present background.
